name: Acetabular labral tear
populations: women with hip dysplasia or hypermobility
athletes in pivoting, kicking and end-range sports
summary: Detachment or splitting of the fibrocartilaginous rim of the hip socket, usually anterosuperior, causing groin pain and clicking. Often secondary to FAI morphology or dysplasia and common without symptoms.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: At least 3 months of exercise-based care; 4–9 months after arthroscopic repair

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: FADIR: high sensitivity, poor specificity; a negative test helps rule out intra-articular pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: 3 T MRI or MR arthrography (Sn ≈0.80–0.89, Sp ≈0.69–0.77)

keyFacts.label: Site
keyFacts.value: Anterosuperior quadrant in about three-quarters of tears

keyFacts.label: Caution
keyFacts.value: Labral tears are seen on MRI in about half of people without hip pain

keyFacts.label: Diagnostic delay
keyFacts.value: Mean 21 months from symptom onset in one surgical series

grading: Histological tear type (Seldes)

keywords.mechanism: Most labral tears result from repetitive loading of the anterosuperior rim: in FAI the femoral head–neck junction shears or crushes the labrum in flexion and internal rotation; in dysplasia the labrum is overloaded as the femoral head translates toward the shallow rim [r7]. An acute tear typically occurs during a forceful twist or pivot on a loaded, flexed hip, a slip into hyperabduction, or end-range hip extension with external rotation, which increases anterior joint force [r8].

name: Achilles tendon rupture
summary: A complete tear of the Achilles tendon, usually in the mid-portion, from a sudden push-off or forced dorsiflexion in a degenerate tendon. It causes a pop, weak push-off and a palpable gap.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Function returns over 6–12 months; calf strength and size deficits can persist beyond a year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 80% return to play (95% CI 75–85%) in a meta-analysis, usually after 6–12 months; criteria-based

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Calf squeeze (Thompson) test: Sn 96%, Sp 93%; Matles Sn 88%, Sp 85%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed if the clinical tests are clearly positive; ultrasound or MRI if uncertain, partial or chronic

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 45 in a Danish registry; men three times as often as women

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 27–31 per 100,000 per year in Denmark (1994–2013), rising in people over 50

grading: Descriptive classification (no universally accepted grading scale)

keywords.mechanism: Most ruptures are non-contact and happen during an explosive push-off: forward acceleration from standing, cross-over cutting or jumping [r2]. At the injury frame in professional footballers the ankle was at end-range dorsiflexion (about 40°), the hip extended and the trunk slightly flexed, with the knee near extension or early flexion (about 22°) and the foot pronated [r2]. The calf contracts forcefully against a tendon that is being lengthened, and the load exceeds the capacity of a degenerate mid-portion [r1].

name: Acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury
populations: young adults, mostly men (trial populations were 91–92% male, mean age about 40 years)
cyclists and other people who fall onto the shoulder
summary: A sprain or dislocation of the joint between the acromion and clavicle, usually from a fall onto the point of the shoulder. Low grades settle without surgery, and the best option for grade III is debated.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Weeks for grades I–II; grade III commonly 2–3 months or more to regain function (clinical convention); function was better with non-operative care than surgery at 6 weeks to 3 months in trials

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; commonly 2–6 weeks (grade I), 6–12 weeks (grade II) and about 3–4 months (grade III) before contact sport (clinical conventions)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Cross-body adduction with observation for clavicular override to detect horizontal instability (consensus-supported; accuracy figures not established)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: True AP or bilateral Zanca view is sufficient for diagnosis; axillary view for posterior displacement

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adults, mean age about 40 years in randomised trials, mostly men

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 9% of injuries to the shoulder girdle; one of the most common shoulder injuries in sport-active people

grading: Rockwood classification (I–VI), as modified by ISAKOS (type III divided into IIIA and IIIB). Descriptions are the classic Rockwood definitions and were not all re-verified in the abstracts reviewed here.

tests: Bilateral comparison of the distal clavicle height and the scapular position
structures: AC joint capsule and AC ligaments
Sternoclavicular joint and subclavian vessels and brachial plexus
Sternoclavicular joint, brachial plexus and subclavian vessels
differentials: Distal clavicular osteolysis or AC joint osteoarthritis
keywords.mechanism: The usual mechanism is a fall or blow directly onto the point of the shoulder with the arm adducted. The force drives the acromion and scapula downwards relative to the clavicle, which is held up by the sternoclavicular joint and trapezius. The AC joint capsule and ligaments stretch and tear first, then the conoid and trapezoid ligaments, and with greater force the deltotrapezial fascia. Indirect injuries from a fall onto an outstretched arm are less common.

name: Acute adductor longus strain
summary: An acute tear of the adductor longus at its proximal tendon, musculotendinous junction or pubic insertion, caused by rapid activation while the muscle is being rapidly lengthened in kicking or change of direction.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Median ~18 days to full training for MRI grade 0–2; ~11 weeks for complete tears/avulsions

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; being clinically pain-free before return is linked to fewer reinjuries

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Palpation of the proximal adductor longus plus resisted adduction (squeeze) reproducing the injury pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI only if a complete tear/avulsion is suspected or for prognosis in elite sport

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adults (median 27 years in an MRI cohort)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% non-contact: change of direction, kicking, reaching, jumping

grading: MRI grading 0–3 (used in the Aspetar adductor cohort studies)

structures: Proximal adductor longus tendon and pubic enthesis
Adductor brevis, pectineus and obturator externus
Adductor longus MTJs (proximal or distal tendon)
Proximal adductor longus tendon / pubic enthesis
differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
keywords.mechanism: Video analysis of acute adductor longus injuries in professional football found that 71% were non-contact and that more than half followed a quick reaction to a change in play [r4]. The injuring actions were change of direction (35%), kicking (29%), reaching (24%) and jumping (12%). Closed-chain injuries (change of direction, reaching) occurred with the hip extended, abducted and externally rotated. Open-chain injuries (kicking, jumping) occurred as the hip moved from extension to flexion and from abduction to adduction [r4]. The common thread is rapid muscle activation during rapid lengthening. In a maximal kick the adductor longus is lengthening fastest (~22 cm/s) near peak hip extension at about 40% of swing, just as it is activating to drive the limb forward [r5].

name: Acute compartment syndrome
summary: SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Rising pressure in a closed leg compartment after fracture, crush or reperfusion causes ischaemia and necrosis. Suspect it early and send for same-day fasciotomy.

keyFacts.label: Urgency
keyFacts.value: Surgical emergency: send to the emergency department now; decompression (fasciotomy) is the treatment

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Depends on timing: normal function followed 68% of fasciotomies done within 12 h of onset versus 8% of later ones (1976 series)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment; clinical signs alone have low sensitivity (13–19%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Imaging does not make the diagnosis. Continuous differential-pressure monitoring: sensitivity 94%, specificity 98% after tibial shaft fracture

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: In 164 cases, 69% had an associated fracture (about half of them tibial shaft); most were men under 35

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Only after surgical decompression, wound healing, fracture union and rehabilitation; no standard criteria

tests: Clinical assessment (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paraesthesia, paresis)
structures: Deep crural fascia and interosseous membrane
differentials: Calf strain or contusion without ACS
Acute arterial occlusion or vascular injury
keywords.mechanism: ACS follows an injury, usually a tibial fracture, direct crush or a reperfusion event. Bleeding or oedema accumulates in a closed osteofascial compartment, so tissue pressure rises toward the diastolic blood pressure and perfusion falls [r2,r10]. Ischaemic muscle and nerve swell and leak, which raises pressure further. Without decompression the cycle ends in necrosis [r2].

name: Acute hamstring strain
populations: older athletes with a previous hamstring injury
summary: A tear of the hamstring muscle fibres, usually the biceps femoris long head near its proximal musculotendinous junction, during high-speed running or an extreme hip-flexion stretch.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Sprint-type 2–8 weeks; stretch-type or intratendinous injuries take much longer

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free palpation, strength, flexibility and maximal sprinting

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Palpation (site and length of tenderness) plus resisted knee flexion; Askling H-test before RTS

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine. MRI if avulsion is suspected, in elite athletes, or for recurrent injury

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 22% of elite male footballers per season

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: 13.9–63.3% within 2 years

grading: British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC)

keywords.mechanism: Sprint-type HSI occurs at maximal running speed, most often in late swing. The hip is flexed and the knee extends rapidly as the shank swings forward. The biarticular hamstrings contract eccentrically to decelerate the shank, so they are long, highly active and lengthening at their peak velocity [r10]. The long head of biceps femoris fails, typically near its proximal musculotendinous junction (MTJ) [r2]. Stretch-type HSI happens during slow, extreme hip flexion with the knee extended and usually affects the proximal semimembranosus tendon [r3].

name: Acute non-specific low back pain (muscle/ligament strain)
populations: people with previous episodes of low back pain
desk-based workers with long sitting exposure
summary: Back pain of under 6 weeks with no identifiable structural cause, usually triggered by a loaded or awkward movement. It improves quickly in most people, but recurs often and is shaped by biopsychosocial factors.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean pain falls from 52 to 23 (0–100 scale) by 6 weeks, then improves more slowly

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: 69% have another episode within 12 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No test identifies the painful tissue; screen for red flags and for radicular signs

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routinely needed: immediate imaging did not improve outcomes in 6 trials (n = 1804)

keyFacts.label: Serious pathology
keyFacts.value: 0.9% (11 of 1172) in one primary care cohort; 8 of the 11 were fractures

keyFacts.label: Burden
keyFacts.value: Leading cause of disability worldwide

grading: Duration-based classification (conventional) and prognostic risk

tests: Straight leg raise or slump test (screen for radicular involvement)
structures: Lumbar nerve roots and dorsal rami
Interspinous and supraspinous ligaments and facet capsules
differentials: Vertebral fracture, infection, malignancy or inflammatory back pain
keywords.mechanism: Most acute episodes are triggered, not caused by one identifiable injury. In a case-crossover study of 999 people with sudden-onset LBP, brief exposures in the 2 hours before onset (manual tasks with heavy loads, awkward postures, caring for live people or animals, moderate or vigorous activity and fatigue during a task) increased the odds of an episode 2.9 to 11.7 times [r7]. The painful tissue is rarely demonstrable, so the animation shows a provocative loaded bend and then the whole set of candidate tissues rather than one failing structure.

name: Acute wry neck (acute torticollis)
populations: people who wake with a stiff neck
people after an awkward movement or sustained posture
summary: A sudden painful loss of neck rotation with the head held to one side and protective muscle spasm. The cause is often unclear, and it usually settles over days to weeks.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Commonly days to a couple of weeks (clinical experience). For acute idiopathic neck pain in general, mean pain fell from 64 to 35 out of 100 by 6.5 weeks but was still 42 at 12 months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria. Needs near-symmetrical pain-free rotation, normal neurological findings and no guarding

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Observation of the head posture and active and passive range of motion, with a neurological screen and a trauma screen (Canadian C-spine rule if any injury)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed for a typical non-traumatic episode; used when there is trauma, neurological signs, fever or a failure to improve

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adults; wry neck is described as common in adults, but age-specific data were not identified

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Not established in the sources reviewed

tests: Observation and palpation for protective spasm
Active and passive cervical range of motion
Neurological screen of the upper limbs
structures: Facet joint capsule or intra-articular tissue (proposed)
Neck muscles (upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, splenius)
differentials: Deep neck infection or retropharyngeal abscess
Cervical dystonia or acute dystonic drug reaction
keywords.mechanism: Acute wry neck has no single, proven mechanism. It often begins on waking or after an awkward movement, with sudden pain and a head held tilted or rotated to one side. The proposed pathway is that a painful tissue, possibly a facet joint capsule (an 'acute facet joint lock') or a muscle, triggers reflex protective spasm of the neck muscles on one side. Spasm holds the head in a fixed position and makes movement painful [r1]. The tissue source is rarely identified, so treat the label as descriptive.

name: Adductor-related groin pain (longstanding)
summary: Longstanding groin pain from the adductor longus origin (adductor tenderness plus pain on resisted adduction) that builds up in kicking and cutting sports and responds to progressive adductor strengthening.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 8–12 weeks of progressive active training, then graded return

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 79% returned to the same level without groin pain after active training

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Adductor longus origin palpation + resisted adduction (squeeze) reproducing pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Rarely needed. MRI changes are common in asymptomatic footballers

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Most common groin entity: 61% of athletes in a groin clinic

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Cumulative kicking, cutting and skating load exceeding adductor capacity

structures: Adductor longus enthesis and proximal tendon
differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
Obturator nerve entrapment / referred lumbar pain
keywords.mechanism: ARGP develops when the cumulative load at the adductor longus origin outpaces its capacity to adapt. Each kick, side-step, reach or skating stride loads the adductor eccentrically at long length and transmits force across the anterior pubis. This happens through an aponeurotic connection with the contralateral rectus sheath, the symphysis capsule and the opposite adductor longus [r8]. Pain usually starts as stiffness after training and progresses to pain during sport, especially with sudden increases in match or training load [r4,r6].

name: Ankle (malleolar) fracture
populations: adolescents and young men in sport
older women (female incidence rises with age)
older adults after a low-energy fall
summary: A fracture of the lateral, medial or posterior malleolus, usually from a twisting injury. Stability depends on the medial structures and the syndesmosis, which decide between casting and surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Bone union takes about 6–12 weeks (clinical convention). At 6 months, ankle scores were still only about 65 of 100 in older adults

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; often 4–6 months or longer after a significant fracture (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ottawa ankle rules rule out fracture (Sn 99.4%, Sp 35.3%); stability is judged on weight-bearing or stress radiographs

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP, lateral and mortise radiographs, ideally weight-bearing; stress views or CT when stability is uncertain

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescent peak in both sexes, then rising incidence in women with age

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 168.7 per 100,000 per year in a Danish population study; lateral malleolus fractures were 55% of all

grading: Weber classification (with Lauge-Hansen mechanism)

tests: Ottawa ankle rules (bony tenderness and weight-bearing)
External rotation stress examination (medial clear space)
Calf examination for deep vein thrombosis
structures: Tibialis posterior, peroneal and flexor tendons, and neurovascular bundle
keywords.mechanism: Most ankle fractures are rotational injuries in which the talus rotates in the mortise and pushes the malleoli or tears the ligaments. In the classic supination–external rotation (SER) pattern, which produces a Weber B fibular fracture at the syndesmosis level, the foot is supinated and the talus rotates externally. In the pronation–external rotation (PER) pattern, the deltoid ligament or medial malleolus fails first and a high Weber C fibular fracture follows [r2]. The sequence of injury (Lauge-Hansen teaching) tells you which medial and posterior structures to suspect, because a fibular fracture that looks isolated may hide a deltoid or syndesmotic injury.

name: Anterior ankle impingement
summary: Anterior ankle pain and limited dorsiflexion from bone spurs or thickened soft tissue pinched at end-range dorsiflexion, common in footballers, dancers and after repeated sprains.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Recurrent (hyper)dorsiflexion and repetitive microtrauma to the anterior ankle

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Conservative care first. After arthroscopy, 74–100% satisfaction in a systematic review; full activity at about 5–10 weeks in one older series

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Anterior joint-line tenderness with pain and a hard end-feel on forced dorsiflexion (clinical diagnosis)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral plus oblique anteromedial radiographs: sensitivity for tibial osteophytes 85% vs 40% on a lateral view alone

keyFacts.label: Typical patient
keyFacts.value: Active adult; average age 31 years in a surgical cohort of 62 patients

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; pain-free loading into end-range dorsiflexion

grading: Osteoarthritis and impingement classification used in arthroscopy studies

structures: Anterior tibial lip and talar neck
differentials: Stress fracture of the anterior tibia or talus
keywords.mechanism: Repeated forced dorsiflexion drives the anterior tibial lip down onto the talar neck. At about 15° of dorsiflexion a triangular synovial and fat-collagen soft tissue component in the anterior joint is squeezed between the tibia and talus [r3]. Over time repetitive microtrauma, such as ball impact on the anteromedial ankle in kickers [r4], and abnormal soft tissue thickening after earlier injury produce spurs and a thickened capsule or synovium, which block end-range dorsiflexion [r2]. The exact cause of the spurs remains debated [r3,r4].

name: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture
summary: A partial or complete tear of the ACL, usually from a non-contact deceleration, landing or cutting movement with the knee near extension and collapsing into valgus.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 9–12 months after reconstruction; rehab-first pathway 3–6 months to stable function

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Not before 9 months post-reconstruction and only once criteria are met

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Lachman (Sn 85%, Sp 94%); pivot shift (Sp 98%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI confirms and identifies associated meniscal, chondral and bone injuries

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 15–25 years

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% non-contact

grading: Anatomical sprain grade (with instrumented / clinical laxity)

structures: Lateral femoral condyle & posterolateral tibial plateau
keywords.mechanism: The classic non-contact ACL rupture happens about 40 ms after initial foot contact during a deceleration, side-step cut or one-leg landing. The knee is only slightly flexed (≈20–30°) and collapses into valgus coupled with internal tibial rotation while ground-reaction forces peak at about three times body weight [r3]. A strong quadriceps contraction near extension adds anterior tibial shear, which the ACL must resist [r2].

name: Anterior shoulder dislocation (with Bankart/Hill–Sachs)
summary: The humeral head is forced forward out of the glenoid, usually in abduction, external rotation and extension, tearing the anteroinferior labrum (Bankart) and often denting the humeral head (Hill–Sachs).

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation over about 3–6 months; after surgical stabilisation about 6 months before contact sport (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not before about 3 months after non-operative care or about 6 months after stabilisation

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Relocation test (LR+ 6.5) and anterior release test (LR+ 8.3)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs before and after reduction; MRI or MR arthrography for labrum and cuff; CT for bone loss

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 20–29 years; 71.8% of emergency department cases are male

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: About 39% overall in adults; markedly higher at 40 years or under

grading: Patterns of structural injury (descriptive; there is no validated grading)

tests: Deltoid isometric contraction and regimental badge sensation
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a force that drives an abducted, externally rotated arm further into external rotation and extension, such as an arm tackle, a fall onto the outstretched or abducted arm, or a forced throw. The humeral head levers over the anteroinferior glenoid rim, tears the anterior capsulolabral complex and comes to rest forward of and below the coracoid. The posterolateral head impacts the glenoid rim on the way, producing a Hill–Sachs impaction.

name: Articular cartilage (chondral/osteochondral) defect of the knee
populations: people after ACL injury or patellar dislocation
summary: A focal loss of articular (hyaline) cartilage, with or without underlying bone, from impaction, shear or chronic overload. It causes activity-related pain and effusion and has very limited capacity to heal.

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Chondral lesions in ~60% of knee arthroscopies; full-thickness defects in 36% of athletes

keyFacts.label: Healing
keyFacts.value: Hyaline cartilage is avascular and has almost no intrinsic capacity to heal

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; MRI with cartilage-sensitive sequences or arthroscopy confirms

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI shows depth, size and subchondral bone; radiographs for loose bodies and alignment

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 76% after cartilage surgery; ~5 months (OAT) to ~12 months (ACI)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 3-month active rehab trial first; 9–18 months after cartilage repair

grading: ICRS (International Cartilage Regeneration & Joint Preservation Society) grade

keywords.mechanism: Acute defects occur when high compressive load is combined with shear: a landing or pivot on a flexed knee, the femorotibial impaction of an ACL pivot-shift, the shear of a patella dislocating and relocating, or a direct blow on a flexed knee. Chronic defects develop when repetitive load exceeds the capacity of cartilage in a joint with malalignment, instability or meniscal loss. The weight-bearing medial femoral condyle and the patella are most often affected [r2,r3].

name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (post-traumatic)
populations: adults after head trauma or concussion
summary: Brief spinning vertigo triggered by head position, caused by displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal, usually the posterior one. Common after head trauma. Diagnose with Dix-Hallpike, treat with the Epley manoeuvre.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: A single Epley manoeuvre resolved vertigo in 56% versus 21% with sham or control (OR 4.42, 5 trials); about 36% recur after treatment

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Dix-Hallpike: vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus confirms posterior canal BPPV. Supine roll test for the horizontal canal

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed when BPPV criteria are met and there are no atypical features; imaging is for central or head-injury red flags

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Lifetime prevalence 2.4% in adults; 8% of 1378 BPPV patients at one tertiary centre had a traumatic cause

keyFacts.label: After head injury
keyFacts.value: Of 179 people with dizziness after mild traumatic brain injury, 10.6% had positional vertigo and BPPV was confirmed in 9

grading: Classification by canal and mechanism (Bárány Society diagnostic criteria) [r5]

tests: HINTS examination (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew)
Cervical vascular and tolerance screen before neck positioning
differentials: Cervical arterial dysfunction or vertebral artery dissection
Vestibular neuritis and other acute vestibular syndromes
Posterior circulation stroke or central positional vertigo
keywords.mechanism: In post-traumatic BPPV, a blow to the head or a sudden deceleration shakes the otolith organs. Otoconia detach from the utricular macula, travel through the common crus and settle in the most dependent canal, the posterior canal, where they collect in the long arm. When the head is tipped back and turned (as in lying down, rolling over or looking up), the crystals move under gravity and drag the canal endolymph, which deflects the cupula and triggers vertigo and nystagmus. This is the accepted canalithiasis model. The mechanical disruption of the otolithic organs after trauma is proposed rather than proven in people [r3].

name: Bone stress injury and RED-S
populations: female athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction
athletes with a sudden rise in training load or a previous bone stress injury
summary: A continuum from stress reaction to stress fracture when load exceeds remodelling capacity. Load, energy availability, bone health and mechanics drive it. Low-risk sites usually heal; high-risk sites need referral.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Across all sites, mean return to sport rose from 41.7 days (MRI grade 1) to 98.5 days (grade 4); cortical-rich sites healed faster than trabecular-rich sites

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: More than 90% of athletes return. Longest at the tarsal navicular (127 days) and femoral neck (107 days); shortest at the posteromedial tibial shaft (44 days)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal bony tenderness with load-related pain that builds over days to weeks, plus a screen for training-load change, energy availability and bone health

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiograph first, often normal early; MRI if radiographs are negative and suspicion remains. MRI grade predicts time to return

keyFacts.label: Risk factors
keyFacts.value: Training-load errors, low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, low bone density, prior bone stress injury and biomechanics

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: In collegiate athletes, 10.5% of 239 female athletes and 27% of 156 male distance runners (mean 1.9 years) sustained a bone stress injury

grading: Kaeding and Miller stress fracture grading (I–V), plus MRI-based BSI grades 1–4 for prognosis

tests: Female Athlete Triad Cumulative Risk Assessment (screen)
structures: Endocrine and nutritional support of bone
differentials: Tendinopathy or muscle strain at the same site
Physeal stress injury in skeletally immature athletes
Infection, tumour or metabolic bone disease
keywords.mechanism: A BSI has no single injury moment. It results from disruption of the homeostasis between microdamage formation and its removal. Microdamage accumulation and the risk of a BSI relate to the load applied to the bone and to the bone's ability to resist load [r1]. Load rises with training volume, intensity and impact forces. Capacity falls when remodelling is impaired, for example by low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction or low bone mass [r4,r7]. The failure site depends on the load pattern: tibial and metatarsal shafts at low-risk sites, or tension-side and trabecular sites that carry more risk [r3,r15].

name: Calcaneal apophysitis (Sever's disease)
populations: active children and adolescents aged about 8–15 years
youth soccer, football and basketball players
children with a higher body mass index
children with a tight calf (gastrocnemius equinus)
summary: Activity-related heel pain in growing children from repeated traction and impact on the calcaneal apophysis. A clinical diagnosis, usually self-limiting, managed with load modification, heel support and calf care.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Self-limiting. In a youth soccer academy, mean time to return to play was 60.7 days (SD 64.9), and longer with recurrence

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Pain-guided and usually without complete rest: modify load, add heel support, then a graded return to full training

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Calcaneal squeeze test (sensitivity 97%) and one-leg heel standing (100%); specificity 100% in one study of 30 children and 15 controls

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed. Sclerosis and fragmentation also occur in pain-free active children; radiographs changed the diagnosis in 1 of 61 patients (a bone cyst)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 8–15 years; mean age 11.8 years in a youth academy cohort

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 0.36 per 100 youth soccer players per year in one academy; up to 16% of paediatric musculoskeletal outpatient conditions

tests: Gastrocnemius–soleus length (ankle dorsiflexion with the knee straight and bent)
structures: Plantar fascia and short plantar muscles
Heel fat pad and heel-strike mechanics
differentials: Acute apophyseal avulsion or calcaneal fracture
keywords.mechanism: Sever's disease has no single injury moment. It develops from repeated loading across an open growth plate: the Achilles tendon pulls on the posterior calcaneal apophysis at push-off, and the heel takes high peak pressure at heel strike [r6,r9]. Because the apophysis is still separated from the heel bone by a growth plate, repeated traction and compression are thought to cause microtrauma and pain at the growth plate. The mechanism is inferred rather than shown directly; there is no histology in the sources reviewed.

name: Calcific tendinopathy of the rotator cuff
populations: people with diabetes or thyroid disease (associated)
summary: Calcium deposition within a rotator cuff tendon, usually supraspinatus, mostly in people aged 30–60. Pain is worst when the deposit is resorbed. Many cases settle with time and conservative care.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Often self-limiting over months, with spontaneous resorption of the deposit common; some people have persistent pain or stiffness (timing varies widely)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based and pain-guided; usually after the painful phase has settled and range and strength are restored (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No validated bedside test for calcific tendinopathy: diagnose from the history plus a deposit on radiograph or ultrasound

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiograph shows the deposit; ultrasound adds morphology and bursitis. Deposits also occur in 7.8% of people with no symptoms

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Age 30–60 years (OR 8.0), more often women (OR 1.5)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Deposits in 7.8% of 734 asymptomatic adults and 42.5% of 485 adults with subacromial pain in one series

grading: Uhthoff stages with ultrasound morphology (no accepted clinical grading)

keywords.mechanism: There is usually no injury. Calcific tendinopathy is thought to be an active, cell-mediated process in which an environment that favours calcification develops within the tendon, followed by spontaneous phagocytic resorption of the deposit. The trigger is not known; theories include local tendon degeneration, repetitive microtrauma, fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and erroneous differentiation of tendon stem cells [r2].

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
aka: median nerve compression at the wrist
populations: people in forceful, repetitive or vibratory manual work
people with diabetes, obesity or thyroid disease
summary: Compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, causing night-time pain, numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers and, in severe cases, thenar weakness. Most start with non-surgical care.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Symptoms are reviewed over weeks to 3 months with non-surgical care; surgery is considered when symptoms persist [Cochrane]

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test is reliable: pooled Phalen Sn 0.57, Sp 0.67; Tinel Sn 0.45, Sp 0.78. Combine history, hand diagram and sensorimotor tests

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Nerve conduction studies (median across the wrist versus a comparison nerve segment) are the most sensitive and accurate neurophysiological test

keyFacts.label: Outcome measure
keyFacts.value: Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (symptom and function scales, 1 = best, 5 = worst)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Trial participants were mostly middle-aged women (84% women in the surgical-versus-non-surgical Cochrane trials)

keyFacts.label: Work link
keyFacts.value: Force, repetition and vibration are associated with CTS; evidence that computer work causes it is insufficient

grading: Practical severity grouping (clinical convention, not a validated cut-off set)

structures: Digital flexor tendons and synovial sheaths
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
differentials: Pronator teres syndrome or proximal median neuropathy
keywords.mechanism: CTS has no single injury moment. Carpal tunnel pressure rises when the tunnel contents (nerve, flexor tendons and their synovial lining) outgrow the space available or when sustained wrist postures and loading increase the pressure on them. The median nerve is then compressed against the tough flexor retinaculum, which forms the roof of the tunnel [r3]. Elevated pressure, ischaemia, mechanical trauma, demyelination and tenosynovial change are all proposed contributors, with mechanical factors considered most likely [r3].

name: Cauda equina syndrome
populations: people with a large central disc herniation or severe canal stenosis
summary: SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Compression of the cauda equina, most often by a large central disc herniation, causes bladder, bowel, saddle sensory and sexual dysfunction. No single sign rules it out; refer the same day.

keyFacts.label: Red flag
keyFacts.value: EMERGENCY: any new bladder, bowel, saddle sensory or sexual change with back or leg pain needs same-day emergency MRI and spinal surgical review

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single sign or test rules CES in or out. In 57 suspected cases only 13 (23%) had CES on MRI, and rectal examination did not discriminate (accuracy 51%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Emergency MRI is the diagnostic test; at least 70% of patients with suspected CES have no cauda equina compression on imaging

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 2.7 per 100,000 per year among people needing emergency decompression in Scotland, peaking at 7.2 per 100,000 in women aged 30–39 years

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Variable. In a 621-patient UK cohort 31% needed a catheter before surgery and 13% at discharge; 65% needed additional health services in the first year

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 30–49 years, and more common in women

grading: Clinical classification by sphincter status

tests: Digital rectal examination (anal tone and sensation)
structures: Intervertebral disc and posterior longitudinal ligament
Lumbar nerve roots (L4, L5) and sacral roots (S1–S4)
Lower limb motor and sensory roots
differentials: Acute low back pain with referred leg pain
Scan-negative CES (functional or other neurological cause)
Conus medullaris lesion or spinal cord compression (myelopathy)
Spinal tumour, infection (epidural abscess), or haematoma
Urinary tract infection, retention from drugs, or constipation
keywords.mechanism: A large herniation of disc material, usually central and posterior, fills the spinal canal at the lumbar levels where the thecal sac contains the cauda equina and compresses all of the lumbosacral roots together. The sacral roots supply the bladder detrusor, the anal sphincters, the pelvic floor and the genital and perineal skin, so compression causes bladder, bowel, sexual and saddle sensory dysfunction. Removing the compression early removes the mechanical and perhaps chemical factors thought to cause progressive neurological damage [r1].

name: Cervical radiculopathy
aka: neck and arm pain with nerve root involvement
populations: younger adults with acute disc herniation
older adults with spondylotic foraminal narrowing
summary: Arm pain, paraesthesia or weakness from compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root, usually C7 or C6, by disc or foraminal change. Most people improve with conservative care.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve: substantial gains in the first 4–6 months; complete recovery took 24–36 months in about 83% of patients in low risk-of-bias studies

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria. Needs pain-free neck and arm movement, normal neurological findings and good neck and scapular endurance

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Spurling's test (specificity 0.89–1.00, sensitivity 0.38–0.97 across studies); a negative upper limb tension test helps rule it out. Findings cluster better than any single test

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI only for red flags, progressive deficit or when surgery is considered; disc bulging is seen in 87.6% of asymptomatic adults

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 48 years; incidence peaks at 50–54 years

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 83.2 per 100,000 per year in a population study (107.3 in men, 63.5 in women)

grading: Root-level clinical patterns (descriptive, not a validated grading; patterns overlap)

tests: Upper limb tension test A (median nerve neurodynamic test)
structures: Ligamentum flavum and superior articular process
Deep neck flexors, scapular stabilisers and thoracic spine
Cervical nerve root (usually C7 or C6)
keywords.mechanism: Cervical radiculopathy usually has no single injury moment. A nerve root is compressed or irritated as it passes through the intervertebral foramen. The foramen is funnel-shaped and narrowest at its entrance zone, where the root is compressed by a protruding disc or osteophytes of the uncovertebral region in front, and by the superior articular process, ligamentum flavum and periradicular fibrous tissue behind [r2]. In older adults the cause is usually foraminal narrowing from spondylosis; in younger adults it is more often an acute disc herniation [r1].

name: Cervicogenic dizziness
populations: older adults with chronic neck pain
summary: Dizziness linked to neck pain or neck movement, thought to arise from disturbed cervical proprioception. A contested diagnosis of exclusion with weak criteria: rule out vestibular, central and vascular causes first.

keyFacts.label: Status
keyFacts.value: A diagnosis of exclusion. The Bárány Society found evidence for a mechanistic link between neck pathology and vertigo lacking and proposed no diagnostic criteria

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No validated test. Cervical torsion, joint position error and smooth pursuit neck torsion tests differ between groups, but accuracy is modest and unproven

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Cannot diagnose it. Use imaging only to exclude central, vascular or structural causes when red flags are present

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Not well defined. In trials, manual therapy reduced dizziness over 6 weeks to 12 months; a meta-analysis rated certainty low to very low

keyFacts.label: Key treatment
keyFacts.value: Manual therapy (for example SNAGs) with neck exercise. High-velocity manipulation is not supported and carries serious adverse-event reports

tests: Cervical torsion test (neck torsion with eyes recorded)
Cervical joint position error (head repositioning accuracy)
Cervical vascular screen before manual therapy (IFOMPT framework)
structures: Cervical afferent pathways to the brainstem
differentials: Cervical arterial dysfunction or vertebral artery dissection
Peripheral vestibular loss or acute vestibular syndrome
Central vestibular disorder or posterior circulation stroke
Orthostatic hypotension, cardiac or medication-related dizziness
keywords.mechanism: The leading proposal is a proprioceptive one. The upper cervical facet joints and suboccipital muscles are rich in proprioceptors whose input is integrated in the brainstem with vestibular and visual information. If neck injury, pain or muscle dysfunction alters this afferent signal, the brain may receive conflicting information about head and body position, which is experienced as unsteadiness, lightheadedness or disequilibrium [r2]. This is a hypothesis. The Bárány Society found no demonstrated mechanism linking the neck to true vertigo, and noted that the observed neck muscle tension in vestibular patients may be a consequence of reduced head movement rather than a cause [r4]. The neurovascular theory has been discredited [r3].

name: Cervicogenic headache
populations: adults with neck pain and headache
people after whiplash or neck trauma
people with sustained postures such as desk work
summary: Headache referred from upper cervical structures (C1–C3) through trigeminocervical convergence. The clinical criteria are contested, and a definite diagnosis needs controlled nerve blocks.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: In trials of manual therapy, exercise or a C1–2 self-mobilisation (a 6-week treatment period in the larger trial), benefit was maintained at 12 months; effect sizes vary and the overall evidence is low-grade

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria. Needs a controlled headache frequency, normal upper cervical rotation and no neurological signs

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Cervical flexion–rotation test: sensitivity 91%, specificity 90% for C1/2-related headache in one small study. A definite diagnosis needs controlled diagnostic blocks

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine; used for red flags or atypical features. Controlled diagnostic nerve blocks, not imaging, establish a cervical source

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adults; peak age not established in the sources reviewed (mean age 36 in one trial)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Estimated at 14–18% of chronic headaches; third occipital nerve headache was found in 27% of 100 patients with chronic whiplash neck pain

grading: Diagnostic certainty (Bogduk and Govind): probable versus definite cervicogenic headache [r1]

tests: Manual examination of the upper cervical joints
structures: C2–3 zygapophysial joint and third occipital nerve
Deep neck flexors (longus colli, longus capitis)
differentials: Secondary headache (intracranial pathology, giant cell arteritis, infection)
keywords.mechanism: Cervicogenic headache has no single injury moment. It arises when a painful upper cervical structure (a C1–2 or C2–3 joint, the C2–3 disc, the suboccipital muscles, or an irritated upper cervical nerve) sends nociceptive input that is felt in the head. Pain from upper cervical joints and muscles can be referred to the head [r1]. The proposed pathway is trigeminocervical convergence. In an animal model, neurones in the C2 dorsal horn received convergent input from the dura and the greater occipital nerve, with receptive fields in the first (ophthalmic) trigeminal division as well as C2 skin and muscle [r13].

name: Chronic ankle instability
populations: athletes with a previous lateral ankle sprain
summary: Recurrent giving way and sprains more than 12 months after a lateral ankle sprain, driven by lasting mechanical laxity and sensorimotor deficits rather than by one structure alone.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: More than 12 months after the first sprain, with recurrent sprains, frequent giving way and persistent symptoms

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Estimates range from 10–20% (Cochrane review) to up to 40% after a first lateral ankle sprain

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Exercise-based rehabilitation is first-line; neuromuscular training improved function at 4 weeks in small trials

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test: combine history of giving way, a validated questionnaire, laxity tests and balance tests

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs to exclude other causes; MRI or arthroscopy for associated cartilage and ligament lesions

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, usually with a brace or tape and ongoing balance training

grading: Contributing-factor classification (mechanical, functional, combined)

differentials: Cavovarus foot or neuropathic cause of giving way
keywords.mechanism: CAI develops when the first lateral ankle sprain leaves lasting mechanical changes (laxity of the repaired ATFL and CFL) together with disrupted afferent input, altered reflexes and motor control, and altered perception of the ankle [r1,r12]. In later landings and cuts the foot reaches the vulnerable inverted position with a smaller trigger and a slower or poorly organised protective response, and the ankle gives way. Each event can add further capsular, cartilage and synovial damage [r10].

name: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome
populations: athletes in running and jumping sports
summary: Reproducible exertional leg pain and tightness from raised compartment pressure, settling quickly with rest. The anterior compartment is most often involved. Treatment is gait retraining or fasciotomy.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: No reliable timeline. A 6-week running-style program gave gains in small series; fasciotomy helped about two-thirds of young athletes

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Symptom-guided graded running after gait retraining; after fasciotomy, per the surgeon's protocol and symptom response

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Dynamic intracompartmental pressure testing, though the pressure criteria overlap the range in healthy people

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Exercise MRI, near-infrared spectroscopy and pressure testing have similar sensitivity; imaging also excludes other causes

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 15–25 years in one review; mean age 26.6 in a surgical systematic review

keyFacts.label: Compartments
keyFacts.value: Anterior 51%, lateral 33%, deep posterior 13%, superficial posterior 3% in surgical series

structures: Deep peroneal nerve and anterior tibial artery
differentials: Lumbar radicular pain or spinal stenosis
keywords.mechanism: CECS develops over weeks of repeated exercise rather than from a single injury. During exercise, intramuscular pressure rises within a compartment bounded by bone, interosseous membrane and deep fascia. The rise compromises circulation, limits muscle function and causes pain [r1]. The precise cause is unknown, and the commonly used pressure criteria do not clearly separate patients from healthy people [r3,r4]. Symptoms subside quickly after stopping [r2].

name: Clavicle fracture
populations: cyclists, contact-sport athletes and snow-sport participants
summary: A fracture of the collarbone, most often the middle third after a fall or blow to the shoulder. Many heal in a sling, but displaced fractures carry a higher nonunion risk, and the value of surgery is debated.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Union takes months: in one trial of displaced fractures mean radiographic union took 16.4 weeks after plating and 28.4 weeks without surgery

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based after radiographic union; commonly 6–12 weeks for non-contact and about 3–4 months for contact sport (clinical conventions)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Bony tenderness, step or crepitus with a neurovascular check, confirmed on AP radiograph

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP radiograph of the clavicle to grade displacement and shortening; CT for complex fractures or suspected nonunion

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Common from childhood to young adulthood; 68% of 535 patients were men

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 2.6% of all fractures and 44% of shoulder girdle fractures; 81% involve the middle third

grading: Allman classification by location, with descriptive modifiers for displacement, comminution and shortening

tests: Palpation of the clavicle for bony tenderness, step and crepitus
Observation for skin tenting and shortening
structures: Deltoid, pectoralis major and the weight of the arm
Sternoclavicular joint and medial clavicular physis
keywords.mechanism: Most clavicle fractures follow a fall or blow onto the point of the shoulder, which loads the clavicle with a lateral compressive and bending force until the middle third fails. Less commonly, the cause is a direct blow to the bone or a fall onto the outstretched arm. After a displaced midshaft fracture, the sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment upward and the weight of the arm pulls the lateral fragment downward, producing shortening and a drooped shoulder. These muscle forces are classic textbook descriptions.

name: Common peroneal (fibular) nerve injury
populations: athletes with knee or ankle ligament injuries
people with knee dislocation or multiligament knee injury
people in casts, splints or tight bandages
people with prolonged squatting, kneeling or leg crossing
people after surgery or prolonged lying
summary: Injury to the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck from a blow, stretch, tight cast or knee dislocation, causing foot drop and dorsal foot numbness. Prognosis varies and the evidence is mostly case series.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Depends on the grade. Neurapraxia is presumed to recover in about 8–12 weeks (a rough guide from a facial nerve series); axonal injury regrows slowly and may need surgery. CPN injury has a poor prognosis compared with other peripheral nerve injuries after multiligament knee injury

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: recovery of dorsiflexion strength and control, with an ankle-foot orthosis in the meantime; no validated criteria

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Weak ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion with numbness over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg; preserved inversion and hip abduction point away from an L5 radiculopathy

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Nerve conduction studies and EMG localise and grade the lesion; ultrasound or MRI for a compressive mass or surgical planning

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Peroneal nerve palsy is the most common entrapment neuropathy of the lower limb; the common peroneal nerve is injured in 16% to 40% of multiligament knee injuries

keyFacts.label: Early referral
keyFacts.value: Complete foot drop after knee dislocation, an open wound, a tense compartment or a progressive deficit; and no recovery after about 3 months

grading: Seddon classification and Sunderland degrees, with surgical outcome graded by useful function

tests: Tinel sign at the fibular neck
Sensory mapping of the first web space and lateral leg
structures: Tibialis anterior and long toe extensors
differentials: Posterolateral corner or multiligament knee injury
Central causes of foot drop (stroke, multiple sclerosis)
Tibialis anterior or extensor tendon rupture
keywords.mechanism: The CPN winds around the fibular neck just under the skin, so it can be compressed against bone by a blow, cast or sustained position, or stretched when the knee or ankle is forced into varus or inversion [r2,r1,r3]. Mild compression blocks conduction without destroying the axon (neurapraxia); greater force or longer duration disrupts axons (axonotmesis), and complete division is neurotmesis [r7,r8].

name: Complex regional pain syndrome
populations: people after distal radius or other limb fractures
people after limb surgery or immobilisation
people after crush or nerve injury
summary: Disproportionate, spreading limb pain with sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor and motor or trophic signs after injury or surgery. Diagnosed clinically (Budapest criteria); treatment evidence is low certainty.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Many cases resolve within the first year and a smaller subset becomes chronic (BMJ review); no model reliably predicts the course in an individual

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Function-led and graded; no validated criteria. Return as pain, swelling, range, strength and normal use of the limb allow

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Budapest clinical criteria: sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.68 against non-CRPS neuropathic pain in one validation study of 113 CRPS-I and 47 comparison patients

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: No test confirms CRPS; tests mainly exclude other causes. Three-phase bone scan: sensitivity 40.0% and specificity 76.5% against the Budapest research criteria in one retrospective series

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Highest incidence in females aged 61–70 years in a Dutch primary-care study; females affected 3.4 times as often as males

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 26.2 per 100,000 person-years (Dutch primary-care database); 3.8% within 4 months of a non-surgically managed wrist fracture in one prospective cohort

grading: CRPS type and Budapest decision rules (no severity grading)

structures: Muscle, joint and bone of the limb
differentials: Cervical radiculopathy or thoracic outlet syndrome
Infection, deep vein thrombosis or inflammatory arthritis
keywords.mechanism: CRPS has no single mechanical mechanism. The trigger is usually a limb injury or surgery, most often a fracture, and in some people a minor injury or none [r3,r4]. After the trigger, an aberrant host response to tissue injury is proposed: a prolonged inflammatory and immune reaction, sensitisation of peripheral and central pain pathways, autonomic and vasomotor dysregulation and maladaptive brain plasticity [r4,r2,r1]. These mechanisms are proposed, they probably differ between people and over time, and none has been proven to be causal in all patients [r2].

name: Cubital tunnel syndrome
aka: ulnar nerve compression at the elbow
ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow
populations: people who hold the elbow flexed for long periods
people with previous elbow trauma or deformity
people who lean on the inner elbow
summary: Compression and stretch of the ulnar nerve behind the inner elbow, worsened by sustained flexion or leaning. It causes ring and little finger tingling, later weakness. Conservative care helps most mild cases.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mild or moderate cases: 51 of 57 patients (89.5%) were improved at 6 months, and information alone, a night splint and nerve gliding did not differ in one RCT

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria exist. Most return once symptoms are controlled and grip and pinch strength are near the other side (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tinel's sign (sensitivity 0.70 and 54% in two studies) and the elbow flexion test (0.32 at 30 s and 46%); elbow flexion plus nerve pressure was most sensitive (0.91 at 30 s) in a 32-patient study

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Electrodiagnosis was abnormal in about 91% and ultrasound in about 95% of clinically diagnosed patients in one retrospective series, so a normal nerve conduction study does not exclude the condition

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 48 years, and 56% men, across surgical series in a network meta-analysis

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Symptoms in up to 5.9% of the general population in one review; the second most common compressive neuropathy after carpal tunnel syndrome

grading: Clinical severity staging (mild, moderate, severe) as used in trials

tests: Tinel's sign over the cubital tunnel
Pressure provocation and combined elbow flexion plus pressure test
Froment's sign, Wartenberg's sign and crossed-finger test
Palpation for nerve subluxation on elbow flexion
structures: Humeroulnar arcade and deep flexor–pronator aponeurosis
Medial collateral ligament and joint capsule
Cubital tunnel retinaculum and FCU aponeurosis
differentials: Ulnar collateral ligament injury of the elbow
keywords.mechanism: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel, behind the axis of elbow flexion [r2]. As the elbow flexes, the nerve is drawn over the epicondyle, the tunnel narrows and pressure rises inside the nerve [r3]. Prolonged or repeated flexion, direct leaning, or a tight or thickened roof therefore combine traction and compression on a nerve that normally glides. Reduced gliding and perineural scarring can then make the nerve more vulnerable still [r2].

name: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
aka: stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment
populations: people in repetitive thumb and wrist work
summary: Stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment (APL and EPB) at the radial styloid, causing radial wrist pain with thumb use. It follows repetitive thumb and wrist loading, infant handling or wrist trauma.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Conservative care first; injection success is documented at 61–83% in a review, and a splint added to injection helps short and mid-term (moderate evidence)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Finkelstein and Eichhoff tests have low specificity; the WHAT test was proposed as an alternative. Accuracy figures were not retrieved

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound can show the intercompartmental septum and made injections more accurate with better outcomes in a review

keyFacts.label: Risk setting
keyFacts.value: 26.8% of 190 infant caregivers had a positive Finkelstein test (small cross-sectional study)

keyFacts.label: After fracture
keyFacts.value: 2.2% (operative) to 3.8% (non-operative) of distal radius fracture patients developed it within a year

keyFacts.label: Nature of the problem
keyFacts.value: Thickening of the first dorsal compartment retinaculum with a degenerative rather than purely inflammatory histology

grading: Practical severity and duration grouping (clinical convention; no validated grading system)

tests: Wrist hyperflexion and abduction of the thumb (WHAT) test
Palpation and resisted thumb extension and abduction
differentials: Trigger thumb (flexor pollicis longus stenosing tenosynovitis)
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury moment. Repeated or sustained thumb abduction and extension combined with wrist ulnar deviation, for example pinch gripping, lifting an infant under the arms, or racquet and tool use, drives the APL and EPB tendons to glide around the radial styloid through a tight fibro-osseous canal. Resisted gliding of these tendons in the canal produces the pain [r1]. In susceptible people the compartment roof thickens and narrows, so the friction rises and pain appears with smaller loads [r3].

name: Degenerative (atraumatic) rotator cuff tear
populations: adults in their 50s and older (trial participants averaged 56–68 years)
people with repetitive overhead work or load
people with a partial-thickness tear or an existing tear on the other shoulder
many people with no symptoms at all
summary: A gradual, age-related failure of a cuff tendon, usually supraspinatus, without a clear injury. Tears are common in people with no pain, and many painful tears improve with exercise.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Pain and function often improve over months with an exercise program (timing is a clinical convention); the tear itself is not expected to heal

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based return to work and recreation; loaded overhead tasks commonly after about 3–6 months of progressive loading (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Lag signs for full-thickness tears (external rotation LR+ 7.2, internal rotation LR+ 5.6); painful arc (LR+ 3.7) for cuff disease in general

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound or MRI: sensitivity and specificity over 0.90 for full-thickness tears, but abnormalities are common in pain-free shoulders

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Cuff abnormality prevalence rises from 9.7% (aged 20 or younger) to 62% (aged 80 or older), with or without symptoms

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Full-thickness tears on ultrasound in 11–17% of two population-based samples of asymptomatic shoulders (low-certainty evidence)

grading: Descriptive classification by thickness, size and muscle quality (no single universally accepted system)

structures: Long head of biceps tendon and rotator interval
Acromion, coracoacromial ligament and subacromial bursa
differentials: Calcific tendinopathy of the rotator cuff
Glenohumeral osteoarthritis or cuff tear arthropathy
keywords.mechanism: A degenerative tear has no single injury. It is thought to arise from cumulative tendon pathology in which load repeatedly exceeds the capacity of an ageing tendon, so that regions of disorganised matrix develop and eventually fail, usually near the supraspinatus footprint. Intrinsic (age-related) and extrinsic (load, subacromial) contributors are both proposed, and no single model explains all presentations [r11,r12].

name: Degenerative meniscal tear
summary: A slowly developing meniscal lesion, usually a horizontal cleavage of the medial posterior horn in people over 35, often an early feature of osteoarthritis. Exercise therapy is first-line, not arthroscopy.

keyFacts.label: First-line care
keyFacts.value: Supervised exercise therapy and education for about 12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Arthroscopy
keyFacts.value: Partial meniscectomy is no better than sham surgery or exercise; not first-line

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs if needed; MRI is usually not indicated first-line

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Present on MRI in 19–56% of people aged 50–90; most are asymptomatic

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Over 35 years; most common from 50 onwards

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Improvement over 3–6 months, continuing to 2 years

grading: MRI meniscal signal grade (intrasubstance to surface tear)

keywords.mechanism: There is no significant injury. With age and cumulative compressive load, the meniscal matrix loses its organisation and strength, so a trivial movement such as rising from a squat with a small twist is enough to complete a tear. Shear stress within the wedge produces a horizontal cleavage, most often in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, where compressive load in flexion is greatest [r1,r10].

name: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)
populations: people starting or returning to exercise
athletes at the start of a season or training block
people trying a new activity or exercise
recreational and elite athletes after eccentric or plyometric sessions
summary: Muscle pain and stiffness that peaks 1 to 3 days after unaccustomed, usually eccentric, exercise. It is self-limiting, a first bout protects later bouts, and most recovery strategies have small effects.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Peak soreness is reported at 48–72 hours; it usually settles within about a week (a common clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Light training can usually continue; reduce intensity and duration for 1–2 days after severe DOMS and re-introduce hard eccentric work progressively

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Diffuse muscle tenderness and pain on stretch or contraction 1–3 days after unaccustomed exercise, with no focal defect and a typical time course

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed. MRI shows increased T2 signal in damaged muscle, but imaging is kept for atypical or severe presentations

keyFacts.label: Risk factors
keyFacts.value: Eccentric or unaccustomed exercise, high intensity or duration, and the start of a season or return after a break

keyFacts.label: Recovery strategies
keyFacts.value: Small, short-lived or uncertain effects; stretching, electrical currents and ultrasound showed no useful effect

tests: Resisted contraction and passive stretch of the affected muscle
structures: Sensory nerve endings (group III and IV afferents)
differentials: Statin-associated or other drug or viral myalgia
keywords.mechanism: DOMS follows exercise that loads muscle in a way it is not used to, most reliably eccentric work: the muscle produces force while it is being lengthened, as in the lowering phase of a squat, downhill running, landings or a first session of resistance training [r2]. The leading model is initial mechanical disruption of sarcomeres, followed by impaired excitation–contraction coupling and calcium signalling, and then activation of calcium-sensitive degradation pathways [r8]. The exact pathway is unknown [r1]. Soreness appears hours later and peaks at 48–72 h because it depends on a sequence of local and systemic responses, not just on the initial damage [r1].

name: Distal biceps tendon rupture
aka: biceps tendon rupture at the elbow
populations: people with a raised body mass index
summary: Acute avulsion of the distal biceps tendon from the radial tuberosity under a sudden eccentric load on a flexed elbow, causing a pop, a Popeye deformity and weak supination. Repair is usually favoured in active people.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: After repair, in a meta-analysis flexion strength reached 94.7% and supination strength 89.2% of the other arm, versus 83.0% and 62.6% without surgery

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, set by the surgeon's protocol; lifting is typically restricted for about 3–6 months (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Hook test: abnormal in 33 of 33 complete avulsions and normal in 45 of 45 uninjured arms (sensitivity and specificity both 100% in one surgeon's 45-patient cohort)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed if the hook test is clear. MRI is used to separate partial from complete tears (sensitivity 92%, specificity 85% in the same cohort)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 46 years; about 95% of cases are in men

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 2.55 per 100,000 patient-years in a US national insurance database

grading: Clinical classification: partial versus complete rupture, with or without retraction

tests: Observation for Popeye deformity and ecchymosis
structures: Lateral antebrachial cutaneous and posterior interosseous nerves
differentials: Partial distal biceps tear or tendinopathy
Bicipitoradial bursitis or anterior elbow impingement
keywords.mechanism: Distal biceps rupture is a sudden failure of the tendon at its insertion on the radial tuberosity. The elbow is flexed and the forearm supinated with the biceps contracting to hold a heavy load. When the load exceeds what the muscle can resist, the elbow is forced towards extension and the biceps lengthens while still contracting. Every patient in a defined cohort described excessive eccentric tension as the arm was forced from a flexed position [r1]. Failure occurs in a tendon with a hypovascular zone that can be nipped between the radius and ulna in pronation, which may have weakened it beforehand [r3].

name: Distal radius fracture
populations: snow, skate and roller sport participants
people after a fall on an outstretched hand
summary: A break of the distal radius, most often from a fall on an outstretched hand; the classic Colles pattern is dorsally displaced. Common in older women and children; needs same-day imaging and a neurovascular check.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Cast or fixation then rehabilitation; most trial outcomes are measured at 12 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Radiographs (PA and lateral); the Lafontaine criteria flag fractures at risk of secondary displacement

keyFacts.label: Older adults
keyFacts.value: Casting is recommended for adults over 65 because long-term outcomes are similar with surgery; trade-offs exist between pain and grip and range (WRIST analyses)

keyFacts.label: Prevention (CRPS)
keyFacts.value: Vitamin C 500 mg daily for 50 days: CRPS RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.33–0.91) in a 3-trial meta-analysis

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Children and older adults carry the greatest risk; 87% of the older-adult WRIST trial participants were women

keyFacts.label: Children
keyFacts.value: Torus (buckle) fractures: a soft bandage was equivalent to rigid immobilisation for pain at 3 days (FORCE)

grading: Descriptive classification (clinical convention) and AO/OTA groups

tests: Radiographic assessment of reduction and alignment (PA and lateral views)
structures: Radial styloid and radiocarpal articular surface
Distal radioulnar joint, TFCC and ulnar styloid
Ulnar styloid and distal radioulnar joint
differentials: Distal radioulnar joint injury or Galeazzi pattern
keywords.mechanism: The classic distal radius fracture follows a fall forward on to an outstretched hand with the wrist forced into extension. The ground reaction force travels up the hand and through the carpus into the distal radius, loading the metaphysis. The volar cortex fails in tension and the fracture line runs dorsally, where compression crushes the dorsal cortex. The distal fragment is displaced and tilted dorsally with radial shortening, which gives the 'dinner-fork' deformity of the Colles pattern (clinical biomechanics).

name: ECU tendinopathy and subluxation
populations: people in repetitive grip and rotation tasks
summary: Pain on the ulnar side of the wrist from the extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) tendon in its sixth-compartment groove: tendinopathy or tenosynovitis from overload, or subluxation when the ECU subsheath fails.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: ECU synergy test: sensitivity 73.7% and specificity 85.7% against sonographic ECU abnormalities (40 wrists, one centre); it was proposed to separate extra-articular ECU pain from intra-articular causes

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Dynamic ultrasound shows subluxation, but MRI instability grading did not relate to symptoms in 105 cases, and 6.6% of 755 asymptomatic people had a snapping ECU

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Initial care is usually non-operative (splinting, load management, strengthening). No randomised trial of splinting, injection or surgery was retrieved

keyFacts.label: Injection
keyFacts.value: In a retrospective series of 55 patients, all 11 with an isolated positive synergy test had more than 90% relief after ECU sheath injection, but only 5 stayed pain free

keyFacts.label: Surgery
keyFacts.value: Subsheath reconstruction is described for refractory instability; reviews and small series only, with a continuing debate between anatomical and non-anatomical techniques

keyFacts.label: Associated injury
keyFacts.value: ECU tenosynovitis was more common in patients with TFCC foveal tears than in controls (43% versus 23%)

grading: Clinical pattern (Montalvan) and MRI subluxation grade (Kim); no validated clinical severity score

tests: Subluxation provocation (supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation)
structures: Ulnar groove of the distal ulna
Ulnar styloid and fifth metacarpal base
differentials: Distal radioulnar joint instability or arthritis
Lunotriquetral ligament injury or pisotriquetral arthritis
keywords.mechanism: In acute instability the ECU is forced out of its groove, and the subsheath is stretched or torn, when the wrist is loaded in flexion, forearm supination and ulnar deviation, for example when a racquet, club or stick hits the ground or a ball at the wrong moment (clinical) [r1,r10]. In a cadaver study the tendon moved ulnarly with forearm supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation, and sectioning the whole subsheath, including its distal extension, caused subluxation [r13]. Tendinopathy and tenosynovitis arise from repetitive loading of the tendon in the same groove, with friction between the sheath and the ulnar groove [r1,r5].

name: Elbow dislocation
populations: people with a high-energy fall or crash
summary: Usually a posterior dislocation of the ulna and radius from a fall on the outstretched hand. Simple cases stay stable after reduction and do best with early guided movement. Fracture-dislocations need surgical review.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: In a 100-patient RCT, early motion gave a larger flexion-extension arc at 6 weeks than 3 weeks of plaster (121° vs 102°), but disability scores were the same at 1 year (DASH 4.0 vs 4.2)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; often about 2–3 months after a simple dislocation and longer after fracture-dislocation (clinical convention; no validated criteria were found)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Stability through the arc of motion after reduction, with a neurovascular check; the lateral pivot-shift apprehension test is the most sensitive test for later posterolateral rotatory instability (no accuracy figures given)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs before and after reduction to confirm congruence and exclude fracture; CT is used when a fracture is suspected (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Highest incidence at 10–19 years (6.87 per 100,000 person-years in US emergency departments)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 5.21 per 100,000 person-years in US emergency departments; males and females were equally affected

grading: Simple versus complex dislocation, with the soft-tissue stages of posterolateral rotatory instability

tests: Post-reduction stability through the arc of motion
Posterolateral rotatory drawer test and stand-up (Regan) test
structures: Lateral ulnar collateral ligament (lateral collateral complex)
Anterior band of the medial collateral ligament
Ulnar and median nerves and brachial artery
differentials: Triceps tendon rupture or olecranon fracture
keywords.mechanism: In a typical fall on the outstretched hand the forearm is planted while the body rotates on it, so the elbow receives an axial load with external rotation (supination) and valgus moments as it flexes. In cadaver specimens this combination produced posterior dislocation in 12 of 13 elbows, with posterolateral rotation of 34–50° and valgus of 5–23° at about 80° of flexion [r2]. Soft-tissue failure progresses from the lateral side to the medial side across three stages, with dislocation as the final stage [r2]. The coronoid then passes behind the trochlea and the olecranon sits behind the humerus. Later MRI series show that the real injury pattern is more variable than this single pathway [r11, r10].

name: Exertional rhabdomyolysis
populations: athletes with a sudden increase in training
people with sickle cell trait or a metabolic myopathy
summary: Muscle breakdown after unaccustomed or extreme exertion (often with heat, sickle cell trait, drugs or supplements): pain, swelling, weakness, dark urine and raised CK. Suspected cases need same-day medical review.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most cases are mild and resolve without sequelae; in endurance-event reports CK and kidney markers usually returned to baseline after about 5.9 days (a pooled review with inconsistent diagnostic criteria)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Individual and guided by symptoms, CK and risk of recurrence; the guidance rests on consensus statements and case series, not trials

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Serum CK of at least 5 times normal, or a urine dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy (one sports-medicine definition); definitions vary, with CK above 1000 IU/L the other commonest cut-off

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose; blood and urine tests decide. MRI shows muscle oedema that can resemble DOMS

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 22.2 cases per 100,000 per year in US military trainees; recurrence 0.08% per person per year in a small cohort

keyFacts.label: Complications
keyFacts.value: Acute kidney injury, compartment syndrome, electrolyte abnormalities and arrhythmias
