grading: Mild versus severe rhabdomyolysis (systematic-review recommendation; no universal grading)

tests: Urine dipstick and microscopy (arranged by a doctor)
Serum creatine kinase (CK) (arranged by a doctor)
structures: Na+/K+ ATPase and the energy supply
differentials: Drug- or statin-related myopathy and inherited metabolic myopathy
keywords.mechanism: ER follows exercise that exceeds what the muscle is conditioned to do, such as high-volume, repetitive or eccentric loading in a person unaccustomed to it, prolonged endurance exercise, or ordinary exercise combined with heat, dehydration, sickle cell trait, certain drugs or an underlying myopathy [r1,r4,r2]. The exact mechanism has not been clearly established, but most studies suggest a cascade of ATP depletion, failure of the sodium–potassium pump, calcium overload and sarcolemma damage that lets intracellular proteins leak into the blood [r1].

name: Femoral neck stress fracture
aka: fatigue fracture of the femoral neck
populations: female athletes with low energy availability
summary: A fatigue fracture of the femoral neck from repetitive loading, usually in runners and recruits. Tension-side fractures can displace and cause avascular necrosis, so suspected cases need urgent MRI.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Compression-side, low grade: about 6–14 weeks; after fixation: 3–6+ months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Graded return to running once walking and hopping are pain-free and imaging shows healing

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; groin pain on hopping or weight-bearing should prompt MRI

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs often normal early; MRI is the definitive investigation

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 3% of sport-related stress fractures

keyFacts.label: Risk
keyFacts.value: High-risk site: delayed diagnosis increases displacement, AVN and career-ending outcomes

grading: Fullerton & Snowdy classification (with Kaeding–Miller grade)

differentials: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
keywords.mechanism: With each foot strike, body weight and muscle forces bend the femoral neck in the frontal plane: the inferomedial cortex is compressed and the superolateral cortex is placed in tension. Thousands of submaximal loading cycles create microdamage faster than targeted remodelling can repair it, so bone resorption temporarily exceeds formation and the neck weakens [r2,r5]. Compression-side injuries begin at the inferomedial neck; tension-side injuries start superolaterally, where crack propagation and poor healing make displacement more likely [r4].

name: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome
populations: male adolescent and young adult athletes
summary: Motion-related hip or groin pain caused by premature contact between the femur and acetabulum, from cam and/or pincer morphology, with positive clinical signs and imaging findings.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: At least 3 months of exercise-based care; 6–12 months after arthroscopy

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: FADIR: high sensitivity (≈94–99%), so a negative test helps rule out; it cannot confirm

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis + lateral (e.g. Dunn 45°) radiographs first; MRI/MRA only if it will change management

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Late adolescence to 40s; cam morphology forms before the growth plate closes

keyFacts.label: Diagnosis
keyFacts.value: Triad: symptoms + clinical signs + imaging (Warwick Agreement)

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Physio-led exercise first line; arthroscopy gives a modest extra short-term benefit in selected patients

grading: Morphological type (Warwick Agreement terminology)

differentials: Acetabular labral tear (without distinct bony morphology)
keywords.mechanism: FAI syndrome is a motion-driven overuse condition rather than a single injury. During hip flexion, especially when combined with adduction and internal rotation, a cam bump at the anterosuperior head–neck junction is levered into the acetabulum, or a pincer rim contacts the femoral neck early [r3,r12]. Repeated contact shears the acetabular cartilage away from the labrum (cam) or crushes the labrum between rim and neck (pincer). Symptoms appear when cumulative load exceeds the capacity of the chondrolabral tissues.

name: Fifth metatarsal fracture (avulsion & Jones)
populations: athletes in football, basketball and soccer
young players in their first seasons of professional sport
summary: A fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal. Zone 1 tuberosity avulsions usually heal with functional care; zone 2 Jones fractures risk delayed union and refracture, and athletes are often offered screw fixation.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Zone 1 avulsion: functional treatment, scores comparable by 6 weeks. Jones fracture: mean union 8.2 weeks with screw fixation versus 13.7 weeks non-operatively

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Athletes after Jones surgery: mean 9.6 weeks (98.4% returned overall); non-operative: mean 13.1 weeks

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal bony tenderness at the fifth metatarsal base after an inversion injury; Ottawa foot rules guide radiographs

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Foot radiographs first. In athletes with a Jones fracture, expert consensus supports MRI for nondisplaced fractures and CT for comminuted or displaced fractures

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Lawrence and Botte zones 1–3 (poor reliability); a 2026 two-part scheme (avulsion versus indirect) had interobserver κ = 0.92

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: The fifth metatarsal is involved in 45–70% of metatarsal fractures; 42% of adult metatarsal fractures in one radiograph series

grading: Lawrence and Botte zones (1–3), with a 2026 two-part avulsion versus indirect scheme

tests: Palpation of the base and the Jones zone
structures: Lateral band of the plantar aponeurosis
Peroneus brevis and lateral plantar aponeurosis
differentials: Os vesalianum pedis or other accessory ossicle
Normal apophysis of the fifth metatarsal base (adolescents)
keywords.mechanism: There are two main mechanisms. A zone 1 tuberosity avulsion typically follows a sudden inversion injury, with the foot plantarflexed and loaded on its lateral border, when the peroneus brevis and the lateral band of the plantar aponeurosis pull the tuberosity off the base [r11,r10]. A zone 2 Jones fracture is an indirect, bending-type injury at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, which can be a single acute overload of the lateral forefoot or a stress fracture from repetitive loading [r13,r10]. Which structure avulses the tuberosity is debated: a cadaver study pointed to the lateral cord of the plantar aponeurosis rather than the peroneus brevis [r11], and a recent classification scheme defines avulsion by the peroneus brevis footprint, which averaged 15 mm in cadavers [r13].

name: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis)
populations: middle-aged adults (mean age at onset about 53 years)
people after shoulder surgery or trauma
summary: A painful, then stiff shoulder from capsular inflammation, fibrosis and contracture, with marked loss of passive external rotation. The natural history is long and variable.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Long and variable; most improvement is early, and about 4 in 10 still have mostly mild symptoms at about 4 years

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mainly an activity problem: return as pain settles and range and strength recover

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Passive external rotation restricted by about 50% or more compared with the other side, with a normal radiograph

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs to exclude other pathology; ultrasound or MRI only if a cuff tear or other cause is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Typically mid-life (mean age at onset about 53 years in one long-term cohort)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Around 10% of people in their fifties; people with diabetes have about 5 times the risk

grading: Descriptive stages (freezing, frozen, thawing) — not a validated grading

tests: Passive external rotation at the side
Resisted tests and cuff screen (external rotation lag and drop-arm)
structures: Rotator interval (coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments)
Axillary recess and inferior glenohumeral ligament
Capsule and synovium of the rotator interval
keywords.mechanism: Most frozen shoulder is primary (idiopathic): there is no single injury. A chronic inflammatory and fibroblastic process develops in the glenohumeral capsule, particularly the rotator interval and axillary recess, which thickens, scars and contracts so that the joint's capacity is reduced and movement, especially external rotation, is lost. A secondary form follows trauma, surgery or immobilisation.

name: Gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome)
populations: women in mid-life and after menopause
people with knee osteoarthritis or low back pain
summary: Persistent lateral hip pain from overload and compression of the gluteus medius and minimus tendons under the iliotibial band, usually in mid-life women, provoked by single-leg loading, hip adduction and side-lying.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months. In the LEAP trial, 8 weeks of education plus exercise gave success in 51 of 66 people, and 51 of 65 at 52 weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free single-leg stance and stairs, abductor strength, then graded walking, running or sport

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: 30-s single-leg stance reproducing lateral hip pain (sensitivity 100%, specificity 97% in a small MRI-confirmed sample); FABER, palpation and resisted abduction also useful

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose. Tendon change on MRI is common in painless hips, and bursitis is present in only a minority

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mid-life. Mean age 54.8 years in the LEAP trial (82% women)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence in adults aged 50–79: unilateral GTPS 15.0% in women and 6.6% in men

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam) with the gluteal tendon MRI categories used in research [r10,r11,r13]

structures: Iliotibial band and tensor fasciae latae
differentials: Hip osteoarthritis or other hip joint pathology
Iliotibial band syndrome and external snapping hip
Isolated trochanteric bursitis or septic bursitis
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury moment. The gluteus medius and minimus tendons run over the greater trochanter and are covered by the ITB. When the hip drifts into adduction, for example in single-leg stance with the pelvis dropping on the opposite side, the ITB presses the tendons against the trochanter. The tendons are then loaded by both compression and tension, which is thought to be most damaging [r1]. Individuals with gluteal tendinopathy have a greater hip adduction moment in walking and stair climbing and altered trunk and pelvic positions [r8,r9].

name: Hallux sesamoid injury (sesamoiditis & fracture)
aka: pain under the big toe joint
populations: adolescent dancers, gymnasts and runners (58 young athletes, 51 of them female, in one series)
athletes with repeated forefoot loading and great-toe extension
football and other athletes after a hyperextension or axial-load injury
people with a bipartite sesamoid, where the cleft can be injured or mistaken for a fracture
summary: Pain under the 1st metatarsal head from the hallux sesamoids: sesamoiditis, stress fracture or acute fracture. Most settle with offloading, but recovery is slow and bipartite sesamoids can confuse the diagnosis.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Slow. In 58 young athletes, 89.8% of fractures were treated without surgery and the mean time to pain-free or cleared for sport was 161.4 days (about 23 weeks)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Young athletes: 84.7% returned to sport. After sesamoidectomy in a systematic review: 94.4% returned, 90.0% to their previous level, at a mean of 11.8 weeks

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness over a sesamoid under the first metatarsal head, with pain on loading and on passive great-toe dorsiflexion; compare with the other foot

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weightbearing radiographs with a sesamoid axial view; early MRI when pain persists; CT to confirm union. A bipartite medial sesamoid (12.7% of feet in one survey) can mimic or hide a fracture

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: No validated grading. Descriptive: sesamoiditis (poorly defined), stress fracture, acute fracture, nonunion, avascular necrosis and the bipartite variant

keyFacts.label: Load
keyFacts.value: The sesamoid complex transmits up to 50% of body weight and more than 300% during push-off

grading: Descriptive diagnostic categories (no validated grading system)

tests: Direct sesamoid palpation with great-toe movement
Vertical Lachman test of the first MTP joint
structures: Sesamoid bone (tibial more often than fibular)
Articular cartilage of the sesamoid and metatarsal head
differentials: Turf toe (first MTP plantar plate injury)
Flexor hallucis brevis or longus tendinopathy or strain
Hallux rigidus or first MTP arthritis
Gout or inflammatory arthritis of the first MTP joint
Intractable plantar keratosis or bursitis under the first metatarsal head
keywords.mechanism: There are two mechanisms. The commonest in athletes is repetitive stress: the sesamoids take very high loads under the first metatarsal head at push-off (more than 300% of body weight), and repeated cycles produce a stress fracture or a painful, inflamed sesamoid [r1,r4]. The second is acute trauma: forced hyperextension of the great toe, or a hard axial load on the forefoot, can fracture a sesamoid or separate the synchondrosis of a bipartite sesamoid, sometimes together with a turf toe injury of the plantar plate [r7]. Which of the two sesamoids is injured depends on the loading pattern; in one nonunion series most fractures were in the tibial sesamoid [r9].

name: High ankle (syndesmosis) sprain
summary: A sprain of the ligaments that bind the distal tibia and fibula, usually from external rotation and dorsiflexion of a planted foot. It recovers more slowly than a lateral sprain, and an unstable injury needs surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Slower than a lateral sprain. Pooled return to play 39 days (non-surgical) and 71 days (surgical) in athletes

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. Stable grade IIa mean 45 days, unstable grade IIb mean 64 days in 64 athletes

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test is accurate. Cluster palpation or dorsiflexion lunge (sensitive) with squeeze (specific, about 85%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs first (clear space and overlap), then stress views or MRI if unsure

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young active adults in collision and cutting sports

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Up to 18% of ankle sprains; much less common than lateral sprains

grading: Stable versus unstable (ESSKA-AFAS), with Calder's subdivision of grade II

tests: Syndesmosis ligament palpation (AITFL and interosseous membrane)
Single-leg hop and pain out of proportion
structures: Talar dome and tibial plafond cartilage
keywords.mechanism: Syndesmosis injuries usually follow an external rotation mechanism [r2]. The foot is planted and the leg rotates internally on it, which is the same as the talus rotating externally in the mortise. Dorsiflexion adds to the load because the wider anterior talar dome pushes the fibula away from the tibia. The AITFL is loaded first, then the interosseous ligament and membrane, and the posterior ligament last; this order is classic cadaveric teaching and is not traced to a source on this page. A concomitant ATFL injury suggests a different, more inversion-type mechanism, and a syndesmosis that is less likely to be unstable [r4].

name: Hip (proximal femoral) fracture in older adults
populations: people with frailty, dementia or falls history
summary: A fracture of the femoral neck or trochanteric region, usually from a sideways fall onto the hip in an older adult with fragile bone. Treated with early surgery, mobilisation within 36 h and multidisciplinary rehab.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most mobility gains in 3–6 months; many never regain pre-fracture mobility

keyFacts.label: Key priority
keyFacts.value: Surgery within 24–48 h and mobilisation within 36 h of surgery

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis and lateral hip radiograph; MRI if clinical suspicion persists despite normal films

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean about 85 years; about 75% women

keyFacts.label: Mortality
keyFacts.value: Roughly 1 in 5 die within a year; 5–8× higher risk of death in the first 3 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Sideways fall with impact on the greater trochanter

grading: Anatomical classification (intracapsular vs extracapsular, displacement)

structures: Soft tissues over the greater trochanter
differentials: Femoral neck stress or insufficiency fracture
Osteoporotic vertebral fracture with referred pain
Acetabular fracture or flare of hip osteoarthritis
keywords.mechanism: The typical hip fracture results from a fall directly sideways from standing height, with impact on the greater trochanter. In a prospective study of 206 consecutive hip fractures, 76% of patients fell directly to the side, 56% had a fresh haematoma over the greater trochanter, and most did not break the fall with an outstretched arm [r3]. The impact load through the trochanter bends and shears the femoral neck or trochanteric region, and osteoporotic bone fails at a load it would once have tolerated.

name: Iliopsoas strain and iliopsoas-related groin pain
summary: Anterior groin pain from the iliacus, psoas or their common tendon and bursa: an acute strain at the MTJ during sprinting or change of direction, or longstanding overload with pain on resisted hip flexion and stretch.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Acute MTJ strain ~1–4 weeks; longstanding tendon or bursal pain 6–12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free resisted hip flexion, stretch, sprinting and kicking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Iliopsoas tenderness + pain on resisted hip flexion and/or hip flexor stretch (modified Thomas)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually not needed. MRI/US for persisting or atypical pain

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Hip flexors account for about a third of acute groin injuries

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Change of direction, sprinting and kicking: rapid hip flexion from an extended hip

differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
keywords.mechanism: Acute iliopsoas strains occur when the muscle is loaded quickly at long length. This happens at the end of hip extension in sprinting or as the athlete brakes and pushes off to change direction, when the iliopsoas is activated eccentrically to stop extension and then concentrically to drive the thigh forward. Iliacus injuries occurred mostly during change of direction, and iliacus and psoas injuries clustered at the MTJ [r3]. Longstanding iliopsoas-related pain develops from repetitive hip flexion under load (kicking, sprinting, sit-ups, dance), which irritates the tendon and the iliopsoas bursa where they glide over the iliopectineal eminence and anterior hip capsule [r8].

name: Iliotibial band syndrome
summary: Lateral knee pain from repetitive loading of the iliotibial band over the lateral femoral epicondyle, typically in runners. It is thought to reflect compression of the tissue under the band rather than simple friction.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Roughly 5–14% of running injuries; the most common lateral knee injury in runners

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Improvement over about 2–8 weeks of treatment in published studies; longer if long-standing

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Pain at the lateral epicondyle at ~30° knee flexion (Noble compression, single-leg squat); no validated accuracy data

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually not needed; MRI or ultrasound excludes other causes of lateral knee pain

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Graded return to running once pain-free with hip strength restored; no validated criteria

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive stance-phase loading with the knee near 20–30° flexion

tests: Single-leg squat or step-down with pain provocation
structures: Fat and loose connective tissue deep to the band
Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus
differentials: Posterolateral corner or lateral collateral ligament injury
Osteochondritis dissecans or lateral femoral condyle bone stress injury
Gluteal tendinopathy or lateral hip pain
keywords.mechanism: ITBS has no single injury moment. It develops from thousands of repeated stance phases in which the knee is only slightly flexed. In nine runners with ITBS the knee was flexed about 21° at footstrike, and the band was thought to impinge at or just below the 30° of flexion traditionally described [r5]. In MRI of volunteers the band was compressed against the lateral epicondyle at about 30° of flexion, as a result of internal rotation of the tibia, and moved laterally off the epicondyle in extension [r3]. Greater peak hip adduction and knee internal rotation preceded ITBS in a prospective study of female runners and may increase strain in the band [r9].

name: Infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad impingement
populations: young athletes in jumping and kicking sports
dancers and gymnasts with knee hyperextension
people after knee arthroscopy or ACL reconstruction
summary: Pain below the patella when the infrapatellar fat pad is pinched between the femur, tibia and patellar tendon, usually in knee hyperextension, causing inflammation, swelling and later fibrosis.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Hyperextension or direct blow pinching the fat pad; patella alta and maltracking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Hoffa's test and pain on passive hyperextension (no accuracy data)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Sagittal MRI shows fat pad oedema; common in asymptomatic athletes too

keyFacts.label: Evidence
keyFacts.value: No treatment trials; management is based on expert opinion and case series

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Usually settles over 6–12 weeks with unloading and exercise

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and young adults; any age after knee surgery

structures: Femoral condyles and anterior tibial plateau
differentials: Fat pad mass or synovial tumour
keywords.mechanism: Impingement occurs when the knee moves into extension or hyperextension and the fat pad is compressed between the inferior pole of the patella, the femoral condyles and the anterior tibial plateau. A sudden forced hyperextension (kicking air, an awkward landing) or a direct blow can bruise it acutely; repetitive end-range extension, standing in recurvatum or a high-riding, laterally tracking patella pinch it repeatedly [r1,r3]. Once inflamed, the swollen fat pad is pinched more easily, creating a self-perpetuating cycle.

name: Inguinal-related groin pain ("sports hernia")
populations: kicking, sprinting and change-of-direction sport athletes
summary: Longstanding pain in the inguinal canal region with canal tenderness and no palpable hernia, typically worse with coughing, sneezing, sit-ups, sprinting and kicking. It is the Doha term for 'sports hernia'.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation-first for 6–12 weeks; ~73% return pain-free at about 10 weeks in rehab cohorts

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: After surgery for failed rehab, about 6 weeks on average in one case series; 90% back by about 3 months in one RCT

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Recognisable pain on inguinal canal palpation (scrotal invagination + Valsalva) and on resisted sit-up

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound (dynamic) to exclude true hernia; MRI for other entities

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mid-20s to early 30s (mean ~28 years in surgical series)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive trunk rotation and hip extension under load: kicking, sprinting, cutting

tests: Inguinal canal palpation with Valsalva (scrotal invagination)
structures: External oblique aponeurosis and superficial ring
Ilioinguinal and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
Adductor longus origin and rectus abdominis insertion
keywords.mechanism: IRGP is an overuse condition of the lower abdominal wall at the inguinal canal. Repetitive, forceful trunk rotation and hip extension during kicking, sprinting and cutting load the external oblique aponeurosis, the conjoint tendon and the transversalis fascia of the posterior inguinal wall. The rectus abdominis and abdominal wall pull the pubis upward while the adductors pull it downward. When this repetitive load exceeds tissue capacity, the posterior wall and aponeurosis attenuate and develop microtears, and the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric or genitofemoral nerves can become irritated or entrapped [r3,r8].

name: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy
populations: people with a Haglund prominence or heel spur
summary: Pain, swelling and stiffness at the Achilles insertion on the back of the heel, from tensile and compressive overload against the calcaneus, often with a bursa or spur. End-range dorsiflexion loading aggravates it.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Slow: months of loading, with about two-thirds satisfied at 4 months in a pilot of modified training; surgery only after failed conservative care

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based graded return after a loading phase that avoids end-range dorsiflexion at first

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness within the distal 2 cm of the tendon at the heel, with pain on dorsiflexion and heel compression

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral weight-bearing radiograph for a spur, calcification or Haglund prominence; ultrasound or MRI for tendon and bursa. Findings track symptoms poorly

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Middle-aged and older adults: mean age 53 in a loading pilot and 59 in a biomechanics study

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 6% of people report Achilles pain in their lifetime, and roughly one-third of that is insertional

grading: MRI grading (Nicholson and colleagues, 2007, as reported by Chimenti and colleagues) with the tendinopathy continuum for load-based staging [r1,r10]

tests: Palpation of the distal 2 cm of the tendon and retrocalcaneal region
Single-leg heel raise and hop provocation
keywords.mechanism: IAT results from combined tensile and compressive overload at the insertion. As the calf pulls, the superficial fibres take high axial tensile strain. As the ankle dorsiflexes, the posterosuperior calcaneus presses into the deep fibres and the retrocalcaneal bursa, causing high transverse compressive strain [r1]. Running loads the Achilles 4 to 6 times body weight [r1]. Compression is thought to drive fibrocartilaginous change and proteoglycan build-up in the tendon [r2].

name: Internal impingement in the overhead athlete
aka: articular-sided cuff and labral lesions in throwers
summary: Pain at the back of the shoulder in late cocking as the cuff undersurface meets the posterosuperior glenoid. Some contact is physiological, the GIRD link is debated and treatment evidence is limited.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Weeks to months of load management, rotation-range work and scapular, cuff and kinetic-chain training; no controlled treatment trials in symptomatic throwers were found

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: After arthroscopic surgery in 135 throwers, 90% returned to sport but only 52% to the previous sport at the same level (mean follow-up 7.9 years)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior shoulder pain reproduced in the throwing position (90° abduction, full external rotation); no validated accuracy figures. Measure internal and total rotation range

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI findings are common in pain-free throwers: the labrum was abnormal in 79% of 28 shoulders of 14 asymptomatic pitchers

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adult throwers: mean age 25 years in the original arthroscopic series of 17 athletes

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Not established; described by surgeons as the leading cause of chronic shoulder pain in overhead throwers

tests: Throwing-position provocation (full external rotation at 90° abduction)
Glenohumeral rotation range and total arc
structures: Posterior capsule and posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
Long head of biceps and superior labrum
keywords.mechanism: In late cocking the arm is abducted to about 90° and maximally externally rotated. The greater tuberosity and the undersurface of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus then contact the posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum, a contact that is physiological in many throwers [r3,r1]. Capsular contracture after repetitive external rotation shifts the humeral head posterosuperiorly, and scapular protraction with glenoid antetilt adds posterior translation of the head; together these predispose to symptomatic internal impingement [r16,r14]. Repetition can then produce articular-sided partial cuff tears, posterosuperior labral lesions and humeral head cysts [r1,r16].

name: Intersection syndrome
populations: people in repetitive wrist-extension or wide-grip lifting work
summary: Pain, swelling and crepitus on the dorsoradial forearm about 4–8 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle, where APL and EPB cross the wrist extensors. The pathology is debated and evidence is mostly case series.

keyFacts.label: Key sign
keyFacts.value: Pain, swelling and crepitus about 4–8 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle, where APL and EPB cross ECRL and ECRB; de Quervain's lies at the radial styloid, further distal

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 5% of one elite national rowing squad developed it over 3 years, losing 20–40% of training time in that period; population incidence was not retrieved

keyFacts.label: Pathology
keyFacts.value: Debated: stenosing tenosynovitis of the second-compartment sheath (13 operated patients) versus friction or fascial compression from the first-compartment muscle bellies; no controlled studies

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Evidence is case reports and small series. Reviews describe rest, a thumb spica splint and NSAIDs, then stretching and strengthening after 2–3 weeks, with injection or surgery for persistent cases

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound and MRI can confirm the diagnosis; an MRI field must include the area 4–8 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle

keyFacts.label: Surgery
keyFacts.value: Reserved for refractory cases in most sources; 5 of 6 elite rowers returned after early surgery (median 7 days to training) in one retrospective series

tests: Palpation of the crossing point with active wrist extension and thumb movement
Resisted wrist extension, radial deviation and thumb extension or abduction
Finkelstein test and radial styloid palpation (to distinguish de Quervain's)
structures: Abductor pollicis longus (APL) muscle belly and tendon
Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) muscle belly and tendon
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis (ECRL, ECRB)
Lister's tubercle and the distal radius
Second-compartment tendons and sheath (ECRL and ECRB)
Peritendinous tissue and fascia at the crossing
differentials: Distal intersection syndrome (second and third compartments)
Radial tunnel syndrome or posterior interosseous nerve entrapment
Lateral elbow tendinopathy or extensor muscle strain
keywords.mechanism: There is usually no single injury moment. Repeated or sustained wrist extension against a gripped handle, with the forearm pronated and the wrist in ulnar deviation, is proposed to make the APL and EPB muscle bellies rub over or compress the ECRL and ECRB tendons at the crossing point, 4–8 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle [r4,r9,r15]. In a cadaver model, pronation with ulnar deviation (without flexion or dorsiflexion) produced the strongest pressure on the distal radius from APL and EPB, and the authors concluded that this position increases the risk of intersection syndrome [r15]. Whether the resulting problem is a friction tenosynovitis of the second-compartment tendons [r1,r5] or a peritendinous inflammation at the crossing is debated.

name: Jersey finger (FDP avulsion)
populations: people who catch a flexed finger on clothing or equipment
summary: Avulsion of the FDP tendon from the distal phalanx when a flexed fingertip is forced into extension, most often in the ring finger. The tendon can retract into the palm, so early surgical review is essential.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Surgical reinsertion, then protected motion. In 29 operated patients, 12 had excellent or good Buck-Gramcko results and 10 had poor results

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Cannot actively flex the DIP joint when the PIP joint is held (FDP test), while PIP flexion is preserved by the FDS

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiograph for a bony avulsion; ultrasound or MRI for a purely tendinous avulsion

keyFacts.label: Digit
keyFacts.value: Ring finger in about 80% of cases in one report; 16 ring and 13 little fingers among 32 operated patients in a series

keyFacts.label: Timing
keyFacts.value: Mean interval from injury to surgery was 6.8 days (range 0–32) in that series

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Leddy and Packer types I–III by level of retraction; types IV and V add associated fractures

grading: Leddy and Packer classification (types I–III), with later additions (types IV and V)

structures: Volar base of the distal phalanx
keywords.mechanism: The finger is flexed and gripping when an outside force pulls the fingertip into extension. This is a forceful hyperextension of an actively flexed DIP joint, so the FDP is loaded eccentrically while it is contracting [r1,r6]. The tendon is avulsed from the volar base of the distal phalanx, with or without a bone fragment [r1]. A computational model of a gripped rod pulled away at sprinting speed produced avulsion at high levels of muscle activation (80% and above) [r6].

name: Knee dislocation (multiligament knee injury)
populations: young adult males in high-energy trauma
summary: Disruption of two or more major knee ligaments, usually both cruciates, from high- or low-energy trauma. The knee may have spontaneously reduced; popliteal artery and peroneal nerve injury must be excluded.

keyFacts.label: Urgency
keyFacts.value: Emergency: limb-threatening popliteal artery injury in about 1 in 5

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ankle–brachial index: <0.90 detected all arterial injuries in one prospective series

keyFacts.label: Nerve injury
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about 25%

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Schenck anatomic (KD-I to KD-V, with C and N modifiers)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 12–18 months; return to any sport about 54%, high-level sport 22–33%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs, CT angiography if ABI <0.90 or abnormal pulses, then MRI

grading: Schenck anatomic classification of knee dislocation (Wascher modification)

keywords.mechanism: Dislocation needs disruption of most of the knee's restraints. High-energy mechanisms (vehicle crashes, falls from height) and sports collisions apply hyperextension, a posterior force on the flexed tibia, or combined varus/valgus with rotation. Hyperextension tends to produce anterior dislocation: the posterior capsule and PCL fail and the popliteal artery, tethered above and below the knee, is stretched. A dashboard blow to the flexed knee produces posterior dislocation, which has a high vascular injury rate [r2]. In people with obesity, a low-energy fall or misstep can dislocate the knee [r6].

name: Lateral ankle sprain
populations: people with a previous ankle sprain
recreational walkers and runners on uneven ground
summary: A partial or complete tear of the lateral ankle ligaments, usually the ATFL first, from a sudden inversion and internal-rotation roll of the foot on landing, cutting or uneven ground.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Pain falls quickly over the first 2 weeks, but 5–33% still report pain at 1 year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria exist. Often weeks for mild–moderate sprains (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Delayed physical examination at 4–5 days (Sn 96%, Sp 84% for ligament rupture); Ottawa ankle rules exclude fracture (Sn 99.4%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine; radiographs only when the Ottawa ankle rules are positive

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Incidence is highest in children, then adolescents, then adults (2.85, 1.94 and 0.72 per 1,000 exposures)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Females 13.6 vs males 6.94 per 1,000 exposures; indoor and court sports carry the highest risk

grading: Clinical sprain grading (I–III; several variants are in use)

tests: Delayed physical examination (4–5 days after injury)
Syndesmosis screen (squeeze and external rotation tests)
structures: Talar dome and distal tibiofibular syndesmosis
keywords.mechanism: Lateral ankle sprains typically occur when the rearfoot undergoes excessive supination on an externally rotated lower leg [r2]. Analyses of real injuries show a sudden inversion with internal rotation of the foot shortly after landing. In five televised tennis cases, peak inversion ranged from 48° to 126° and peak internal rotation from 35° to 99°, with the foot only slightly inverted at the moment of landing [r3]. In a laboratory handball side-step, inversion and internal rotation peaked 130–180 ms after initial contact [r11]. The classic teaching of plantarflexion plus inversion is a useful simplification, but the sagittal-plane position was variable: the tennis cases fluctuated between plantarflexion and dorsiflexion in the first 0.5 s after foot strike [r3], and the handball case showed considerable dorsiflexion [r11].

name: Lateral elbow tendinopathy (tennis elbow)
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin (ECRB) at the lateral epicondyle, causing pain with gripping and wrist extension. Managed with education, load modification and progressive exercise.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Usually self-limiting, but symptoms can persist beyond 1 year in up to 20% of people

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not time-based: pain-free gripping and tolerance of full work or sport load; most people in trials were much improved by 6–12 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness at the lateral epicondyle plus pain on resisted wrist or middle-finger extension and gripping. In one small study (30 patients, all with the condition) sensitivity was 0.97 for Cozen's test and 0.87 for Mill's test

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis. In 21 patients MRI showed tendinosis signal in 18, but the severity of the signal did not match symptoms

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 45–54 years in a Finnish population sample; equally common in men and women

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence of definite lateral epicondylitis 1.3% in adults aged 30–64; incidence fell from 4.5 to 2.4 per 1000 people between 2000 and 2012 in one US cohort

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, used alongside pain and function

tests: Palpation of the lateral epicondyle and ECRB origin
structures: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brachioradialis
Radial collateral and lateral ulnar collateral ligaments
Posterior interosseous nerve and arcade of Frohse
Capitellum, radial head and annular ligament
differentials: Posterolateral rotatory instability or lateral collateral ligament injury
Intra-articular pathology (synovial plica, osteoarthritis, loose body)
Referred pain from the shoulder or trigger points
keywords.mechanism: Lateral elbow tendinopathy has no single injury moment. It develops when repeated or sustained gripping and wrist extension load the common extensor origin faster than the tendon can adapt. During a grip the extensor carpi radialis brevis and its neighbours hold the wrist extended and stable while the finger flexors squeeze, so a heavy or repetitive grip (hammering, lifting, a racquet stroke, mouse work) transmits high tension to the origin at the lateral epicondyle [r2,r4]. When load repeatedly exceeds capacity, the tendon moves from a reactive state towards disrepair and degeneration [r9].

name: Lateral patellar dislocation
summary: The patella leaves the trochlear groove, almost always laterally, usually in a twisting knee injury. The medial patellofemoral ligament tears, and the patella often relocates on its own.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 23 per 100,000 person-years overall; about 148 per 100,000 at age 14–18

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: Roughly 17–40% after a first dislocation, depending on risk factors, population and follow-up

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Medial patellar tenderness and patellar apprehension; no validated accuracy data identified

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs for fracture or loose body; MRI shows MPFL injury and bone bruises

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation over about 3–6 months; criteria-based, not time-based

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Most uncomplicated first dislocations are managed without surgery

grading: Clinical pattern of patellar instability (WARPS versus STAID)

structures: Medial patellomeniscal ligament and medial retinaculum
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a non-contact twisting injury. The foot is planted, the knee is flexed, and the femur rotates internally over the fixed tibia as the knee collapses into valgus. The quadriceps pull then drives the patella over the lateral trochlear ridge. A direct blow to the medial patella can also cause it. No mechanism-of-injury study was identified in the sources reviewed, so the sequence below is the standard clinical description. It fits the injury pattern on MRI: medial patellar restraint damage with bone bruises of the lateral femoral condyle and the medial patella [r4].

name: Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) injury
populations: athletes in football, rugby and soccer (axial load or twist on a plantarflexed foot)
people with high-energy or crush trauma, including polytrauma
male athletes (ligament injuries predominated in the athlete consensus review)
summary: A midfoot ligament or fracture-dislocation injury at the tarsometatarsal joints, often from axial load on a plantarflexed foot. Easily missed without weightbearing imaging; stability decides treatment and arthritis risk.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Stable injuries: non-weightbearing immobilisation for about 6 weeks, then graduated weightbearing. Unstable injuries need fixation or arthrodesis, and the surgeon's protocol governs

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Athletes with stable, nondisplaced ligament injuries managed nonoperatively mostly return within 6–10 weeks; one pooled athlete review reported 2.8 months versus 4.5 months for bony injuries

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Midfoot pain, pain on midfoot squeeze and inability to bear weight after axial load or a twist through a plantarflexed foot; plantar bruising is a classic sign

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Bilateral weightbearing radiographs first; CT or MRI if radiographs are normal and suspicion remains. Non-weightbearing films missed 24% of injuries in one reader study

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Nunley and Vertullo stages I–III (weightbearing radiograph based); recent reviews favour a stable versus unstable framework

keyFacts.label: Long-term risk
keyFacts.value: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis in about 33% after medial tarsometatarsal injuries in one meta-analysis; non-anatomical reduction was the main modifiable factor

grading: Nunley and Vertullo stages I–III (athletes, weightbearing radiographs), within a stability-based framework

tests: Piano-key test (first and second ray stress)
Single-leg heel raise and weightbearing tolerance
structures: Lisfranc ligament (interosseous, medial cuneiform to second metatarsal base)
Dorsalis pedis artery and deep peroneal nerve
Second metatarsal base and medial cuneiform
Articular cartilage of the TMT joints
differentials: Cuboid, cuneiform or other midfoot fracture
keywords.mechanism: The athlete mechanism is axial compression or a twist through a plantarflexed foot, with the heel raised and the body weight carried through the forefoot and midfoot [r3]. A fall onto the heel, a missed landing or a player landing on the back of the leg loads the midfoot, and the metatarsal bases are forced out of line with the tarsus. The Lisfranc ligament, which ties the second metatarsal base to the medial cuneiform, tears or avulses a fleck of bone, and the gap (diastasis) between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal opens. Direct crush injuries and high-energy trauma produce more severe fracture-dislocations and have poorer outcomes [r6].

name: Long head of biceps tendinopathy
populations: people with rotator cuff tendinopathy or tears
manual workers who lift and work overhead
summary: Anterior shoulder pain attributed to the long head of biceps tendon, in the bicipital groove or inside the joint. It usually coexists with rotator cuff changes and is rarely an isolated pain source.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Variable and poorly documented; a loading program is usually trialled for about 3 months before surgery is considered (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; commonly 3–6 months for overhead or heavy-lifting sport (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No clinical test is diagnostic: Yergason's test had LR+ 2.56 and LR− 0.70 in a systematic review of 30 studies; Speed's test sensitivity was 32% to 63% across studies

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound is highly specific for complete rupture and dislocation of the tendon; MRI sensitivity for tendinosis or partial tear is 67.8% and specificity 75.9%

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Rises with age (about 4% per year in an MRI series); everyone aged 85 or over in that series had cuff and biceps tendinopathy

keyFacts.label: Co-pathology
keyFacts.value: In one ultrasound study 55.3% of people with biceps tendinitis also had a rotator cuff injury

structures: Bicipital groove, transverse humeral ligament and tendon sheath
Rotator interval, coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments (pulley)
differentials: Anterior shoulder instability or subscapularis tear
keywords.mechanism: LHB tendinopathy usually develops gradually from repeated loading rather than from one injury. Each time the arm elevates and rotates, the tendon slides through the bicipital groove and rotator interval, and it works eccentrically to decelerate the arm in throwing and lowering tasks (clinical reasoning). When load repeatedly exceeds the capacity of a tendon that is ageing or already stressed by a rotator cuff problem, tendon structure and pain sensitivity change [r1]. Because the tendon, the cuff and the rotator interval share the same space, it is often not possible to say which structure is the source of pain.

name: Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
populations: people with heavy lifting or prolonged sitting exposure
summary: Displacement of disc material through a fissured annulus, usually posterolaterally at L4–5 or L5–S1, irritating a nerve root and causing leg-dominant pain. Most cases settle without surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve with non-surgical care; 95% of trial patients reported recovery at 1 year, with or without early surgery

keyFacts.label: Natural history
keyFacts.value: Herniations often resorb: pooled 70.4% overall, higher for extrusion and sequestration

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Straight leg raise (pooled sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.28 in surgical samples); crossed SLR specificity 0.90

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI only if surgery or injection is planned, or red flags are present; protrusions are seen in 29–43% of pain-free adults

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 30–50 years; male to female about 2:1

keyFacts.label: Red flag
keyFacts.value: Cauda equina syndrome is a same-day emergency

grading: Morphological classification of herniation (standard nomenclature)

keywords.mechanism: Repeated or sustained lumbar flexion combined with compressive load, often with some axial rotation, increases tensile strain on the posterior and posterolateral annulus while the nucleus is squeezed backwards. Cumulative loading creates annular fissures, the nucleus tracks outward along them and eventually pushes through the outer annulus toward the spinal canal or foramen, where it contacts a nerve root.

name: Lumbar facet joint pain
summary: Back pain thought to arise from the lumbar facet joints, typically with degeneration in older adults. It cannot be diagnosed reliably from history, examination or imaging; only controlled blocks can confirm it.

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Up to 15% of chronic low back pain on controlled blocks; 15% had at least 50% relief after a confirmatory block in one cohort of 176

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No history or examination finding is diagnostic; none of the tests for facet pain was informative in a systematic review

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Facet osteoarthritis on CT in 59.6% of men and 66.7% of women in a community sample, with no association with back pain

keyFacts.label: Diagnostic standard
keyFacts.value: Controlled blocks; single uncontrolled blocks had a 38% false-positive rate and a positive predictive value of 31%

keyFacts.label: Radiofrequency denervation
keyFacts.value: Conflicting: moderate evidence of short-term benefit in a Cochrane review, but no clinically important benefit in the facet joint MINT trial

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Older adults; prevalence of facet-mediated pain rises with age

grading: Diagnostic certainty (there is no accepted clinical grading)

tests: Laslett clinical prediction rules for a screening block
Neurological screen and straight leg raise or slump
structures: Medial branch of the dorsal ramus
differentials: Osteoporotic vertebral fracture, infection or malignancy
keywords.mechanism: Facet joint pain is usually an insidious, degenerative problem and not the result of a single injury [r2]. Ageing, disc degeneration and spondylolisthesis alter how load is shared across the segment, so the facet joints bear more compressive and shear load, especially in extension and rotation [r3]. The joint capsule and synovium become irritated and the cartilage degenerates, and the innervated capsule can generate pain, although how much any given joint contributes to pain is unreliable to judge clinically [r2,r4].

name: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
populations: people with a congenitally narrow canal
summary: Degenerative narrowing of the lumbar canal and recesses that squeezes the cauda equina or roots, causing buttock and leg symptoms on standing and walking that ease with sitting or bending forward.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Both exercise-based care and surgery improved function over 2 years in trials; 57% of surgical candidates given physical therapy crossed over to surgery

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: History: no pain when seated (LR 7.4), relief on bending forward (LR 6.4), bilateral buttock or leg pain (LR 6.3)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI when surgery or injection is considered; radiological stenosis is found in a pooled 11% of asymptomatic people and severity does not track symptoms

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Older adults; acquired CT stenosis rose from 20.0% (relative, under 40 years) to 47.2% at 60–69 years

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Clinically diagnosed in a pooled 11% of the general population, 25% in primary care (high risk of bias)

keyFacts.label: Red flag
keyFacts.value: New bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms or rapidly progressive weakness need same-day emergency assessment

grading: Anatomical zone (descriptive); there is no accepted clinical severity grade

tests: History: bilateral buttock or leg pain
keywords.mechanism: Lumbar spinal stenosis has no injury moment. Years of disc dehydration and bulging, facet hypertrophy and ligamentum flavum thickening reduce the cross-sectional area of the canal and recesses at one or more levels, and a canal that is only just adequate at rest becomes inadequate when the spine extends or is loaded. In patients with sciatica or neurogenic claudication, axial loading in slight extension reduced the dural sac area in 66 of 84 patients [r13], which fits the clinical pattern that upright standing and walking provoke symptoms while sitting or bending forward relieves them [r2].

name: Mallet finger
populations: people with finger-jamming injuries at home or work
summary: Loss of active DIP extension after the terminal extensor tendon ruptures or avulses a dorsal bone fragment, typically when a ball forces an extended fingertip into flexion. Continuous splinting is the main treatment.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Continuous DIP extension splinting for 6–8 weeks (6 for acute, 8 for chronic injuries in the trials), then graded motion

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: The fingertip droops and the patient cannot actively extend the DIP joint, although it can be passively straightened

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: A lateral finger radiograph shows any bone fragment and volar subluxation of the distal phalanx

keyFacts.label: Outcome
keyFacts.value: Mean DIP extensor lag was 5.7° after surgery and 7.6° after nonsurgical care in a review of 44 studies

keyFacts.label: Surgery
keyFacts.value: Generally indicated for volar subluxation or fragments over one-third of the joint surface, but the advantage is not clearly proven

keyFacts.label: Splint choice
keyFacts.value: Prefabricated orthoses carried about three times the risk of skin complications of other orthoses (RR 3.17)

grading: Doyle classification (the most widely adopted system, with fracture subtypes by joint surface involved)

tests: Passive DIP extension and swan-neck screen
structures: Dorsal base of the distal phalanx
keywords.mechanism: The classic injury is a sudden forced flexion of an actively extended DIP joint, for example a ball hitting the tip of an outstretched finger (clinical). The terminal extensor tendon is stretched beyond its capacity at its insertion on the dorsal base of the distal phalanx. It either ruptures or avulses a fragment of bone [r2]. The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) is then unopposed, so the fingertip droops into flexion (clinical anatomy). If the finger is not held in extension, the tendon heals long, and the lag persists [r2].

name: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain
summary: A sprain or tear of the medial collateral ligament from a valgus force, usually a blow to the outside of the knee. Most isolated tears, even complete ones, heal well with early functional rehabilitation.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I ~2 weeks; grade II 3–4 weeks; grade III 6–8+ weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean lay-off 23 days in professional football

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Valgus stress at 30° (pain and laxity together: LR+ 6.4 with history)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually clinical; MRI if laxity in extension or suspected ACL, meniscal or posteromedial injury

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% contact: a blow to the lateral knee

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Most common knee ligament injury in professional football

grading: Clinical grading (valgus stress at 30° flexion, opening compared with the other side)

tests: Valgus stress test in full extension
structures: Deep MCL and posterior oblique ligament
keywords.mechanism: The typical mechanism is a valgus force: a blow to the lateral side of the knee, or a fall or tackle onto it, with the foot planted and the knee slightly flexed, where the superficial MCL is the dominant restraint [r1,r4]. External rotation of the tibia often accompanies the valgus load and adds stress to the deep MCL and posteromedial structures. Non-contact valgus-rotation injuries (cutting, skiing) also occur, and higher-energy or more extended-knee injuries may involve the ACL [r1].

name: Medial elbow tendinopathy (golfer's elbow)
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor–pronator origin at the medial epicondyle, causing pain with wrist flexion, forearm pronation and gripping. Managed with education, load change and exercise.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Responds well to non-operative care in most people. In 20 refractory patients given eccentric exercise plus other measures, treatment lasted about 6 weeks on average (uncontrolled)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not time-based: pain-free gripping, pronation and full swing or throwing load; in a surgical series 9 of 30 elbows needed more than 6 months to reach maximum improvement

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness at the medial epicondyle plus pain on resisted forearm pronation (positive in 28 of 30 elbows in a surgical series) or resisted wrist flexion (12 of 30)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis. Use it to exclude other causes, such as a UCL injury, an avulsion or a bony problem

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 40–60 years; usually less common than lateral elbow tendinopathy

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence of definite medial epicondylitis 0.4% in Finnish adults aged 30–64, compared with 1.3% for lateral epicondylitis

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, used alongside pain and function [r10]

tests: Palpation of the medial epicondyle and common flexor origin
Passive wrist extension stretch (elbow extended, forearm supinated)
Valgus stress and moving valgus stress tests
Ulnar nerve screen (Tinel's sign and elbow flexion test)
structures: Pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis
Flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis
differentials: Posteromedial olecranon impingement or elbow osteoarthritis
keywords.mechanism: Medial elbow tendinopathy has no single injury moment. Flexor–pronator degeneration develops with repetitive forced wrist extension and forearm supination during activities that demand wrist flexion and forearm pronation, so the muscle group works eccentrically as the wrist is forced the other way and then concentrically to flex and pronate [r1]. In golf the trail arm flexes and pronates through impact; in throwing the load peaks in late cocking and early acceleration [r1]. When load repeatedly exceeds capacity the tendon moves from a reactive state towards disrepair and degeneration [r9].

name: Medial gastrocnemius strain ("tennis leg")
populations: people with a previous calf strain
summary: A strain of the medial gastrocnemius, usually at the musculotendinous junction, from a sudden push-off or lunge with the knee straightening while the ankle is dorsiflexed. It causes sharp calf pain and often a haematoma.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean return to play about 19 days for gastrocnemius strains (25 days for soleus) in elite Australian football; longer if severe

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; running criteria are stricter than for other muscle strains, and recurrence is common

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Medial belly or musculotendinous tenderness, painful single-leg heel raise, and pain on stretch with the knee straight; exclude Achilles rupture (Thompson) and DVT

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not always needed. Ultrasound or MRI if the diagnosis is uncertain: medial gastrocnemius rupture in 67% of 141 'tennis leg' referrals

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Classically middle-aged recreational athletes; increasing age is one of the strongest risk factors

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Calf strains made up 3.6% of injuries over 5 years in one soccer study cited in a review

grading: Traditional clinical grading I–III (Dixon), with MRI-based alternatives: British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) and the Munich consensus classification [r1,r8,r9]

tests: Palpation for medial belly and musculotendinous junction tenderness or a defect
Resisted plantarflexion and passive dorsiflexion, with the knee extended versus flexed
structures: Medial gastrocnemius (distal musculotendinous junction and aponeurosis)
differentials: Lumbar radiculopathy (S1) or other referred calf pain
keywords.mechanism: In the classic mechanism the knee extends while the ankle is dorsiflexed, as in a push-off from a lunge or an explosive start. This puts the biarticular medial gastrocnemius at its longest length just as it contracts hard [r1]. The muscle fails at its distal musculotendinous junction or aponeurosis, and blood tracks between the gastrocnemius and soleus. In an ultrasound series of 141 patients with a clinical diagnosis of tennis leg, the medial head was ruptured in 66.7% and the plantaris tendon in only 1.4% [r6].

name: Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints)
summary: Exercise-related pain along the distal posteromedial tibial border, tender over 5 cm or more. The pathology is uncertain and sits on a bone stress continuum; load management is the first-line approach.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months. In one athlete study a graded running program alone took a mean of about 92 days to reach 18 min of pain-free running

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: no border tenderness, pain-free walking, then a graded run progression. No validated MTSS-specific criteria exist

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Diffuse tenderness over at least 5 cm of the posteromedial tibial border. Two clinicians agreed on the diagnosis (kappa 0.89)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose. MRI oedema was present in only 43.5% of symptomatic legs; use MRI to exclude a stress fracture

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 4–35% of athletes and military personnel; 5–35% of runners

keyFacts.label: Treatment evidence
keyFacts.value: No single treatment is supported by trials free of high risk of bias

grading: MRI bone stress continuum (Fredericson) [r3]

structures: Soleus and flexor digitorum longus attachments
differentials: Lumbar radicular pain (disc herniation) or nerve entrapment
keywords.mechanism: MTSS has no single injury moment. It develops over weeks of repetitive running or jumping load on the distal posteromedial tibia. Each foot strike sends an impact load up the tibia [r11], and the calf muscles then work through stance and push-off while the shaft bends under the combined ground reaction and muscle forces. The soleus, flexor digitorum longus and deep crural fascia attach along the symptomatic border, so fascial traction may add to the bone load [r4]. When load repeatedly outpaces remodelling, bone resorption exceeds formation in the cortex [r1].

name: Meralgia paraesthetica (LFCN entrapment)
aka: lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh neuropathy
populations: people after hip, pelvic or spinal surgery
people who wear tight belts, harnesses or equipment at the waist
summary: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment near the ASIS: burning, numbness or tingling over the anterolateral thigh without weakness. Many cases settle; evidence for injection and surgery is limited.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: In the single natural-history study in a Cochrane review, 20 of 29 cases (69%) improved without treatment; most patients in a surgical series were managed conservatively

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Usually unrestricted once symptoms allow; remove the compressing factor (belt, harness, posture) and return as tolerated

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Pelvic compression test: sensitivity 95% and specificity 93.3% in one surgical series of 45 patients, and 86.7% and 93.0% in a small case-control study of 30 patients

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Nerve conduction studies, ultrasound or MR neurography support the diagnosis; MR neurography sensitivity was at least 71% and specificity at least 94% in one study of 11 patients and 28 controls

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 50 years in a population-based series, with increasing incidence with age and BMI

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 32.6 per 100,000 patient-years in Olmsted County, Minnesota, and 247 per 100,000 in people with diabetes

tests: Sensory mapping of the anterolateral thigh
differentials: Lumbar disc herniation with L2–L3 radiculopathy
Hip joint pathology (femoroacetabular impingement or labral tear)
Gluteal tendinopathy or greater trochanteric pain
keywords.mechanism: MP is an entrapment or traction injury of the LFCN where it leaves the pelvis, passing medial to the ASIS and under or through the inguinal ligament (standard anatomy) [r2]. Sustained external pressure at the waist (belt, waistband, harness), abdominal bulk or swelling, a tight ligament with hip extension, or surgical injury can compress or stretch the nerve; the result is a conduction block and abnormal firing in the sensory fibres, giving burning, tingling or numbness over the anterolateral thigh [r1]. The details of the mechanism are inferred from general compressive neuropathy models; the sources read did not test them in MP.

name: Metatarsal stress fracture
populations: female and male athletes with low energy availability
athletes with a sudden rise in training load
summary: A repetitive-load bone injury of the metatarsal neck or shaft, most often the second or third. Most heal with load reduction and graded loading, but training load and energy availability must be addressed.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Low-risk sites usually heal with load reduction and graded return; mean return to sport rose from 41.7 days (MRI grade 1) to 98.5 days (grade 4) across all bone stress injury sites

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: More than 90% of athletes return. A return-to-run program can start once the athlete is pain-free in daily activities for 5 consecutive days

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal bony tenderness over the second or third metatarsal neck or shaft, with pain on hopping and push-off

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs have low sensitivity early; MRI is highly sensitive and specific, and its grade predicts time to return

keyFacts.label: Risk factors
keyFacts.value: Training-load errors, low energy availability, prior bone stress injury, a higher arch, and long metatarsals or abnormal foot motion

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Stress fractures make up 0.7–20% of sports medicine clinic injuries; the tibia, metatarsals and fibula are the most frequent sites

grading: Kaeding and Miller stress fracture grading (I–V), plus MRI-based BSI grades 1–4 for prognosis

tests: Bony palpation of the metatarsal neck and shaft
Percussion or tuning-fork test over the metatarsal
structures: Second and third metatarsal neck and shaft
Intrinsic foot muscles and toe flexors
differentials: Freiberg's infraction or MTP synovitis and plantar plate injury
Extensor tendinopathy or dorsal foot soft-tissue overload
keywords.mechanism: A metatarsal stress fracture develops from repetitive loading of the forefoot at push-off, without a single injury moment. The metatarsals act as levers and are bent by ground-reaction and muscle forces thousands of times per run. A BSI results from disruption of the balance between microdamage formation and its removal: it depends on the load applied to bone and on bone's ability to resist load [r1]. When training load rises faster than the bone and its muscles can adapt, microdamage accumulates, a stress reaction develops, and a cortical fracture line can follow. The second and third metatarsals are the most common sites in runners and recruits [r3].

name: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the main body of the Achilles tendon, 2–6 cm above the heel, causing pain and stiffness with running and jumping. It is managed with progressive calf and tendon loading.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months, not weeks: 12-week loading blocks improved symptoms in RCTs, and full recovery can take up to a year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based graded return to running and jumping after a loading block; recurrence is common during the return phase

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Localised mid-portion thickening and tenderness; arc sign (pooled Sp 88%, Sn 42%) and Royal London Hospital test (+LR 3.84)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis; ultrasound or MRI if a tear or other pathology is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Active adults; mean age about 50 in the trials reviewed

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 1.85 per 1000 patients registered with Dutch GPs; a sport link was recorded in only 35% of cases

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, to be used alongside pain and function [r7,r10]

structures: Retrocalcaneal bursa and Kager's fat pad
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury moment. In running, the Achilles tendon is stretched as the ankle dorsiflexes over the planted foot, then recoils as the calf drives the ankle into plantarflexion at toe-off. Each cycle loads the tendon several times body weight, and thousands of cycles are repeated per run. When load rises faster than the tendon's capacity, or recovery between sessions is too short, the mid-portion matrix cannot keep up and becomes painful and thickened (general biomechanics; no single source).

name: Morton's neuroma
aka: common plantar digital nerve perineural fibrosis
populations: middle-aged women (female:male about 5:1 in one review)
people who wear tight, narrow or high-heeled footwear (proposed)
runners and dancers with high forefoot loading (clinical observation)
adults referred to foot and ankle surgeons with forefoot pain
summary: Perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve, most often in the 3rd web space, causing burning forefoot pain and a pebble-in-the-shoe feeling. The evidence for injection and surgery is limited and mixed.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Variable. In one review, footwear changes and orthoses gave convincing results only within about 4.5 months and for neuromas smaller than 5–6 mm; surgery is considered when nonoperative care fails

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: No validated criteria. Return as forefoot loading is tolerated in suitable footwear; after surgery, follow the surgeon's protocol (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Web space tenderness with a squeeze: the modified thumb–index finger squeeze test had sensitivity 0.96 and LR– 0.04 in one study; patient-reported clicking was specific (0.96)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Often not needed. In one series, clinical diagnosis had 98% sensitivity, ultrasound 90% and MRI 88%; up to 25% of people have asymptomatic neuroma-like findings

keyFacts.label: Pathology
keyFacts.value: Benign perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve, usually in the third intermetatarsal space; it is not a true neoplasm

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 87.5 versus 50.2 cases per 100 000 UK females versus males; third web space affected in 43–86% of neuromas

tests: Modified web space tenderness test (thumb–index finger squeeze test)
Sensory testing of the adjacent toe sides
Lesser MTP vertical drawer and joint palpation
structures: Common plantar digital nerve (third web space)
differentials: Metatarsophalangeal joint synovitis or plantar plate tear
Freiberg's disease or osteochondritis of the metatarsal head
Rheumatoid or gouty nodules, tenosynovial giant cell tumour
Plantar fat pad atrophy or forefoot overload metatarsalgia
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury. Four theories are cited: chronic repetitive trauma, ischaemia, entrapment of the nerve beneath the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament, and intermetatarsal bursitis [r3,r10]. The common pathway proposed is repeated compression and traction of a common plantar digital nerve in the web space, particularly when the forefoot is squeezed in tight footwear or the toes are extended at push-off. The nerve then develops perineural fibrosis, which makes it thicker and easier to pinch [r3,r2]. The cause remains controversial [r2].

name: Multidirectional shoulder instability
populations: people with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder
summary: Symptomatic shoulder instability in more than one direction, usually atraumatic and often with generalised laxity. Rehabilitation is the first treatment but its evidence is limited; surgery is for failures.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Supervised rehabilitation over 12 weeks to 6 months: in a randomised trial the Watson program beat the Rockwood program at 12 and 24 weeks (12 weekly sessions plus home exercise)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: No MDI-specific return-to-sport criteria were found; use criteria on strength, scapular control and absence of apprehension

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Sulcus sign with Beighton score, apprehension and load-and-shift; sulcus sign and load-and-shift had only moderate intertester reliability (kappa 0.39–0.73 across six tests)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Clinical diagnosis. MRI or MR arthrography for labral tears or to exclude other pathology; imaging does not diagnose MDI

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Teens and young adults: median age 24.3 years (range 9–56) across 861 shoulders in a systematic review

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No reliable incidence found. After physiotherapy, 21% (52 of 253) needed surgery in a systematic review

structures: Rotator interval capsule and coracohumeral ligament
Scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, lower and middle trapezius)
keywords.mechanism: MDI usually has no single injury moment. A lax capsule and incompetent dynamic stabilisers, from congenital or acquired causes [r3], allow the humeral head to translate under little load: downward when carrying, forward in overhead or throwing positions, and backward when pushing or pressing. Scapular positioning is often altered, with reduced scapular lateral rotation, increased internal rotation and antero-inferior decentring of the head [r12]. Repeated end-range loading, or one minor event in an already lax shoulder, then produces pain, apprehension and subluxation or dislocation in more than one direction [r2].

name: Olecranon bursitis
populations: manual workers who lean on their elbows
people with gout or rheumatoid arthritis
people on steroid therapy or with alcohol misuse (septic risk)
summary: Inflammation and fluid in the subcutaneous olecranon bursa from pressure, friction, a direct blow, crystal disease or infection. Aseptic cases usually settle with conservative care; septic bursitis needs same-day review.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: In a 90-patient trial of non-septic bursitis, 83% treated with compression and NSAIDs had resolved by 4 weeks; time to resolution was about 2–3 weeks across groups

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: swelling settled, full pain-free elbow movement and tolerance of padded contact; no standard time frame

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Fluctuant swelling over the olecranon with a painless, full range of elbow movement. In septic cases tenderness (88% vs 36%), erythema (83% vs 27%), warmth (84% vs 56%) and fever (38% vs 0%) were more common, but the findings overlap

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed for uncomplicated cases. Ultrasound helps to separate bursitis from cellulitis; radiographs after trauma or for spurs and fractures

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adults, mostly men; mean age 52 years in a series of septic bursitis (80% male)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 29 per 100,000 person-years in a military population, rising to 97 per 100,000 in combat roles

grading: Aetiological classification (septic versus aseptic; acute traumatic, chronic microtraumatic, chronic inflammatory) [r3]

tests: Inspection and palpation of the bursa for fluctuance and warmth
Ultrasound of the bursa and skin
differentials: Cellulitis over the elbow without bursitis
Gout or other crystal or inflammatory arthritis
Olecranon fracture or elbow injury after a fall
Elbow dislocation or other joint injury
Elbow joint effusion or inflammatory arthritis
keywords.mechanism: The olecranon bursa is a thin sac between the point of the elbow and the skin. It reduces friction between them, and when the skin is repeatedly pressed or slid against bone the bursal lining becomes irritated and fills with fluid. The same bursa can be injured by a single direct blow, which causes bleeding into it, or inoculated with bacteria through broken skin [r3,r5]. Chronic microtrauma is the most common cause of superficial bursitis [r3].

name: Osgood–Schlatter disease
aka: traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle
summary: A traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in growing adolescents. Repeated quadriceps pull through the patellar tendon causes activity-related pain below the knee. Usually self-limiting, but it can persist.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Up to about 10% of adolescents; higher in sports-active adolescents

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Boys 12–15 years, girls 8–12 years (older estimates); sex difference may be shrinking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness and a prominence over the tibial tuberosity; pain on resisted knee extension and kneeling. Clinical diagnosis

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not usually needed; lateral radiograph or ultrasound if atypical

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
