keyFacts.value: Self-limiting with physeal closure, but adolescents in one cohort had pain for a mean of 21 months before enrolling

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Education, load management and progressive strengthening. 80% reported success at 12 weeks in a case series

grading: Radiographic progression (descriptive; no validated clinical grading)

tests: Kneeling or direct pressure over the tuberosity
structures: Infrapatellar fat pad and deep infrapatellar bursa
differentials: Hip pathology referring to the knee (for example slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
keywords.mechanism: OSD has no single injury moment. Jumping, sprinting, kicking and landing load the quadriceps repeatedly, and each contraction pulls through the patella and patellar tendon onto the tibial tuberosity. During growth that attachment is on a secondary ossification centre rather than mature bone, so it is the weak link [r1,r4]. Repetitive traction produces microtrauma and irritation at the apophysis. Radiographs show irregularity and separation of the apophysis early on, and fragmentation later [r1]. The apophysis fuses as growth finishes, and most symptoms settle [r1,r3].

name: Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the knee
summary: A focal disorder of subchondral bone, usually on the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle in active adolescents, that can loosen the overlying cartilage and bone. Stable juvenile lesions often heal with offloading.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 12–19 years; about 4 times more common in males

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 9.5 per 100,000 in 6–19-year-olds

keyFacts.label: Typical site
keyFacts.value: Medial femoral condyle (64%), classically its lateral aspect

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs including a notch (tunnel) view; MRI to assess size and stability

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Stable juvenile lesions: about two-thirds progress to healing in 6 months of offloading

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No reliable clinical test; diagnosis is radiological

grading: Stability and skeletal maturity, with the ROCK arthroscopic classification

keywords.mechanism: There is usually no single injury. Repetitive impact and shear load the subchondral bone of the femoral condyle faster than it can remodel, particularly in adolescents whose secondary ossification centre is still maturing. One theory is that the tibial spine impinges on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle when the tibia rotates internally. The bone beneath the cartilage weakens, becomes ischaemic and separates from the parent bone, and the cartilage may then fissure and detach [r3].

name: Patella fracture
summary: A fracture of the kneecap from a direct blow (fall onto the knee, dashboard) or a sudden eccentric quadriceps contraction. Displaced fractures disrupt the extensor mechanism and usually need fixation.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 13 per 100,000 per year; highest in women aged 60–80

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Active straight-leg raise: inability suggests extensor mechanism disruption

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP, lateral and skyline radiographs; Ottawa rules include isolated patellar tenderness

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Bone union takes weeks to a few months and varies with age and fixation; strength and function 6–12 months

keyFacts.label: Surgery threshold
keyFacts.value: Extensor mechanism disrupted, or >2–3 mm step-off / >1–4 mm displacement

keyFacts.label: Common complication
keyFacts.value: Symptomatic implant removal in about 30% after fixation

grading: Descriptive classification by pattern and displacement (AO/OTA 34)

tests: Active straight-leg raise / extensor lag test
keywords.mechanism: Two mechanisms dominate [r2]. A direct blow to the front of the flexed knee, typically a fall onto a hard surface or a dashboard impact, compresses the patella against the femoral trochlea and tends to produce comminuted (stellate) fractures, often with the retinacula intact. An indirect mechanism, a sudden eccentric quadriceps contraction while the knee is flexed (for example, stumbling and trying to stop a fall), loads the patella in tension like a beam over the trochlea and produces a transverse fracture whose fragments are pulled apart when the medial and lateral retinacula also tear. Many falls combine both.

name: Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee)
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the proximal patellar tendon, causing pain at the base of the kneecap with jumping, landing and deceleration. It is managed with progressive tendon loading.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months, not weeks: in a 24-week trial, VISA-P improved by 28 points with progressive loading (18 with eccentric exercise)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. In a chronic, mostly previously treated cohort, 43% (progressive loading) and 27% (eccentric) had returned in the 24-week trial

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Load-related pain at the inferior pole of the patella; single-leg decline squat reproduces it. Palpation PPV 68% in symptomatic tendons

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound or MRI show tendon change but correlate poorly with symptoms; not needed to make the diagnosis

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young athletic adults (mean age 24 in the main RCT); more common in men

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence 14.2% in elite athletes across sports; 44.6% in elite volleyball

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, to be used alongside pain and function [r3]

tests: Palpation of the patellar tendon at the inferior pole
differentials: Patellar tendon rupture or partial tear
keywords.mechanism: Patellar tendinopathy has no single injury moment. It develops from repeated high loading of the knee extensor mechanism in the stretch–shortening cycle. On landing or deceleration the quadriceps contracts eccentrically as the hip, knee and ankle flex, so the patellar tendon lengthens and stores elastic energy; on take-off or push-off it recoils and returns that energy [r1]. When this loading is repeated faster than the tendon can adapt, load exceeds capacity and the tendon's structure changes [r2]. Landing strategy matters: in drop jumps, athletes with previous jumper's knee landed more stiffly, with higher knee angular velocity and loading rates [r8].

name: Patellar tendon rupture
populations: people with previous patellar tendinopathy or repeated steroid injections
people with systemic disease or on medicines that weaken tendon (less often)
summary: A sudden tear of the patellar tendon below the kneecap, usually in active men, often after a jump landing or a violent quadriceps contraction. It needs urgent surgical repair, and delay worsens results.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: About 6 months to return to sport in one cohort of 46 repairs (mean 5.88 months, 87.0% returned); full strength can take longer

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Systematic review of 757 patellar tendon repairs: 88.9% returned to play, with 80.8% returning to the same level. NFL extensor mechanism ruptures: 56.8% returned, median 11.3 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Palpable defect below the patella and inability to straight-leg raise. A palpable defect was found in all 24 NFL ruptures

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral radiograph for a high-riding patella (patella alta); ultrasound or MRI when the diagnosis is unclear

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age 32–45 across repair series; 93.8% male in a review of 970 patients

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 0.68 per 100,000 (quadriceps tendon rupture 1.37 per 100,000)

grading: No validated grading system. Descriptive classification by completeness, site and timing (clinical convention)

tests: Straight-leg raise and extensor lag test
differentials: Osgood–Schlatter disease or tibial tubercle avulsion
keywords.mechanism: Patellar tendon rupture is usually an indirect injury from a sudden, forceful quadriceps contraction against a flexed knee, most often an eccentric overload during a jump landing, deceleration or cut, often with valgus [r2,r11,r7]. In a video analysis of professional-athlete extensor mechanism ruptures, the knee was flexed and the ankle plantarflexed at injury, with a tendency to valgus, and about 70% were non-contact [r11]. A pre-existing degenerate tendon lowers the load needed to fail: 11 of 24 NFL ruptures had antecedent symptoms [r2]. The tear can occur at the inferior pole of the patella, in the mid-substance, or as a distal avulsion [r5,r3].

name: Patellofemoral pain
summary: Pain around or behind the kneecap, provoked by squatting, stairs or running, which arises when repeated patellofemoral load exceeds tissue capacity. Managed with education and hip-plus-knee exercise.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Anterior knee pain on squatting (PFP present in about 80% of people positive); there is no definitive test

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Education plus a physical treatment beats wait-and-see at 3 months, but many people still have symptoms years later

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, with modified activity usually continued throughout rehab

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose; structural findings correlate imprecisely with pain

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and young adults; common in female athletes, runners and military recruits

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Annual prevalence 22.7% in the general population and 28.9% in adolescents (systematic review)

tests: Single-leg squat / step-down with movement analysis
Clarke's (patellar grinding) test and apprehension test
structures: Hip abductors, external rotators and foot–ankle complex
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury event. PFP develops when repeated or suddenly increased patellofemoral joint load, usually through a flexed, weight-bearing knee (mid-stance of running, stair ascent or descent, squatting, jump landings), exceeds the capacity of the joint's tissues [r3]. As the knee bends under load, the quadriceps must produce more force to control the flexion moment, and that force and the patellar tendon pull compress the patella into the trochlear groove. Hip adduction and knee abduction (valgus) during running and landing are associated with PFP, although prospective evidence is limited and inconsistent [r8,r9].

name: Pectoralis major rupture
summary: A rupture of the pectoralis major, usually the tendon avulsing from the humerus in a strong man during a heavy bench press or forced tackle. It causes chest and axillary bruising, a lost axillary fold and weak adduction.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: After repair, return to resisted training about 9 weeks and to full sport commonly 3 to 6 months (case reports and a case series; clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean 11.1 weeks to competition after repair in 20 Australian Football League players; one footballer returned to full contact at 87 days and a wrestler to competition at 24 weeks

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Loss of the anterior axillary fold and chest contour with resisted horizontal adduction; no accuracy figures were found for clinical tests

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI is used to confirm the site and extent of tear and tendon retraction; ultrasound is an alternative (accuracy figures not found)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Men aged 20 to 40 years; mean 26.5 years in elite Australian footballers

keyFacts.label: Strength after surgery versus none
keyFacts.value: Peak torque 99% of the uninjured side after repair versus 56% without repair in one small retrospective comparison

grading: Descriptive classification by tear location and completeness (no single universally accepted system)

tests: Observation of the axillary fold with resisted horizontal adduction
Palpation of the tendon and the humeral insertion
Resisted horizontal adduction and internal rotation strength test
structures: Pectoralis major tendon insertion on the humerus (lateral lip of the bicipital groove)
Pectoralis major muscle belly and MTJ
Biceps brachii and its long head tendon
differentials: Pectoralis major muscle strain or contusion
Acute cardiac event or other chest cause
keywords.mechanism: The classic description is a forceful eccentric contraction of the pectoralis major while the arm is abducted, extended and externally rotated (textbook description). Weightlifting and the bench press are the commonest mechanism overall [r2], and in filmed AFL injuries the commonest mechanism was horizontal hyperextension [r3]. The load exceeds the tensile strength of the tendon-bone junction, and the tendon, most often the sternocostal head, avulses from the humerus [r3]. A forced traction injury can produce a similar tear [r4].

name: Peripheral nerve injury (Seddon/Sunderland)
populations: people with high-energy trauma, fractures or dislocations
athletes with severe ligament or multiligament knee injuries
people with lacerations or penetrating injuries
people with sustained or repeated pressure over a nerve at a tunnel or bony prominence
summary: Injury to a peripheral nerve, graded by Seddon (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis) and Sunderland. Recovery depends on the grade and is slow at about 1 mm a day; no sign of recovery means early referral.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Neurapraxia is presumed to recover within about 8–12 weeks (a figure from a facial nerve series, so treat it as a rough guide); after axonal injury, axons regrow at about 1 mm a day, so recovery takes months and depends on the distance to the target muscle

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. Protect the denervated limb, track reinnervation, and rebuild strength as muscles recover; return depends on grade, site and muscle recovery

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Motor and sensory loss in one nerve's territory with a typical mechanism; document a baseline and repeat serially, with an advancing Tinel sign as a clinical sign of regrowth

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Electrodiagnostic study (nerve conduction and EMG) localises and grades the injury; useful information can be obtained in the first week, though it is conventionally delayed to about 3 weeks

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No general incidence figure was identified in the abstracts reviewed; the common peroneal nerve is injured in 16% to 40% of multiligament knee injuries

keyFacts.label: Early referral
keyFacts.value: Refer when there is no clinical or electrical sign of recovery, with an open wound or progressive deficit, or with a proximal injury, where decisions must be made more quickly

grading: Seddon classification (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis) and Sunderland classification (degrees I–V)

tests: MRC manual muscle testing of each muscle
keywords.mechanism: Nerves are injured by cutting, crushing, stretching or by ischaemia [r1]. In sport and trauma the commonest mechanisms are a direct blow or sustained pressure that compresses the nerve against bone or in a tight tunnel, and traction when a joint is forced beyond its range, as when varus stress at the knee stretches the common peroneal nerve around the fibular neck [r7,r1]. Mild compression blocks conduction without destroying the axon (neurapraxia). Greater force or longer duration disrupts axons, causing Wallerian degeneration beyond the lesion, and complete disruption leaves a gap that does not recover without surgery [r1,r2].

name: Peroneal tendinopathy
populations: people with chronic lateral ankle instability
summary: Load-related pain and thickening of the peroneus brevis or longus tendon behind the lateral malleolus or at the cuboid groove. It is often linked to a cavovarus foot or lateral ankle instability.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: No trial data. Treatment is based on case series and expert opinion; most are managed non-operatively first

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria. After surgery for tears, 46% returned to sport in one series

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Pain on palpation of the tendons behind the lateral malleolus with resisted eversion or dorsiflexion; no accuracy data found

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs for foot shape, ultrasound for dynamic assessment, MRI for tears and associated lesions

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Active adults with repetitive loading; no reliable age data found

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: True incidence unknown; frequently missed. Only 60% of 40 peroneal disorders were correctly diagnosed at first examination in one study cited in a review

grading: Anatomical classification of peroneal tendon disorders (no validated clinical grading)

tests: Palpation of the peroneal tendons with resisted dorsiflexion and eversion
Resisted eversion and passive inversion stretch
Anterior drawer, talar tilt and standing hindfoot alignment
differentials: Sinus tarsi syndrome and subtalar pathology
keywords.mechanism: Peroneal tendinopathy has no single injury moment. It develops when repetitive load, often with a supinated or varus foot and a lateral ankle that moves too much, exceeds the capacity of the tendons [r1,r2]. Both tendons turn around the back of the lateral malleolus in the retromalleolar groove, and the longus turns again under the cuboid. These turns concentrate compression and friction. Peroneal tendinopathy is likely to result from overuse, whereas subluxation more often follows forceful peroneal contraction during sudden dorsiflexion, for example landing or stopping abruptly [r2].

name: Persisting post-concussion symptoms
populations: adolescents and young adults after concussion
people with a history of migraine
summary: Concussion symptoms that outlast the expected window (beyond 10–14 days in adults, 4 weeks in children). Causes are multifactorial: neck, vestibular, eye movement, exertion and mood. Treat the drivers.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Variable and not well defined. Most people improve with targeted rehabilitation, but trial evidence is low to moderate quality

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About one-third of children (35.1%, 95% CI 26.3–45.0%, in 13 studies); 31.0% at 28 days in one large paediatric cohort

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No test is diagnostic. Diagnosis relies on symptom report with standardised scales, plus a multimodal examination of neck, vestibular, eye-movement, exertion and mood

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually normal. Use it for red flags or atypical features, not to confirm persisting symptoms

keyFacts.label: Key treatments
keyFacts.value: Subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise (commonly 20 minutes at 80% of the symptom-threshold heart rate), cervicovestibular rehabilitation, and collaborative care with CBT

tests: Graded exercise test (Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test)
structures: Upper cervical spine and neck muscles
Autonomic nervous system and cerebral blood flow regulation
differentials: Acute concussion within the expected recovery window
Depression, anxiety, PTSD or sleep disorder
Intracranial pathology (for example subdural haematoma, hydrocephalus)
keywords.mechanism: PPCS begins with an ordinary concussion: an impulsive force to the head produces a neurometabolic disturbance with rotational strain of the brain. In most people the brain recovers within weeks [r10]. In others, symptoms persist because the injury also involved or unmasked other systems: the neck, the vestibular and oculomotor systems, autonomic control of exercise, sleep and mood. These processes can sustain each other, so symptoms continue even after the initial disturbance has settled [r1]. The sequence below is a clinical model, and the links are plausible but not all proven.

name: Pes anserine tendinopathy / bursitis
aka: medial knee pain below the joint line
populations: middle-aged and older women, often with knee osteoarthritis
people with obesity or type 2 diabetes (association inconsistent)
runners and athletes who repeat knee flexion
adolescents with a medial proximal tibial osteochondroma (rare)
summary: Pain over the medial proximal tibia where sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert. The bursitis label is contested: imaging rarely shows bursal fluid, and osteoarthritis and meniscal pain overlap.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Not established. Trials followed patients for only 1–8 weeks after injection or shockwave, and no trial of exercise or stretching was found

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: No validated criteria. Return is guided by pain, tolerance of loading and exclusion of other medial knee pathology (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness over the pes anserine insertion. Compared with MRI, clinical diagnosis had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5% in 156 patients

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI showed pes anserine bursitis in only 2.5% of 509 symptomatic knees; ultrasound showed it in 20% of knees in a symptomatic osteoarthritis cohort

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mostly middle-aged to older women in the published series. All 22 cases in one case-control study were women with a mean age of 62

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Anserine bursa tenderness was reported by 33.3% of 3,654 people with or at risk of knee osteoarthritis. True bursitis is far less common

tests: Clinical diagnosis of pes anserine tendinitis-bursitis (history plus tenderness over the insertion)
Resisted knee flexion with tibial internal rotation
Medial joint-line palpation and McMurray test
structures: Medial collateral ligament and medial joint line
differentials: Degenerative medial meniscal tear or medial compartment osteoarthritis
Tibial stress fracture or bone injury of the medial plateau
Snapping pes anserine tendons or a ganglion cyst
keywords.mechanism: Pes anserine pain has no single injury moment. The usual proposal is overuse: repeated knee flexion and valgus loading make the conjoined tendons pull and glide over the medial proximal tibia, irritating the tendon insertion or the bursa beneath it [r5]. Valgus knee deformity was associated with the diagnosis (OR 5.2) in a small case-control study [r12]. This mechanism is a clinical model: the tissue source of pain has not been shown, and no biomechanical study was identified.

name: Physeal (growth plate) fracture — Salter–Harris
populations: children and adolescents with open growth plates
adolescent athletes around the growth spurt
children who fall onto an outstretched hand
young gymnasts and climbers (physeal stress injuries)
summary: A fracture through or involving the growth plate in a skeletally immature child, classified Salter–Harris I to V. Most heal, but growth disturbance and angular deformity can follow, so follow-up matters.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Union usually takes weeks (a common clinical convention); high-risk fractures need radiographic monitoring for at least 1 year for growth disturbance

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, after union and orthopaedic clearance; contact and high-impact sport come last

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness over an open growth plate after a fall or twist. Among radiograph-negative lateral ankle injuries in children aged 5–12, MRI found a distal fibular Salter-Harris I fracture in only 3.0%; most were ligament sprains

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs in at least two planes (oblique views can show a metaphyseal extension); CT or MRI for intra-articular fractures, occult injury and physeal bars

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: In 1124 children with epiphyseal fractures, Salter-Harris II was most common (1002 of 1147 fractures); type V was rare (1 case); the distal radius was the commonest site

keyFacts.label: Growth disturbance
keyFacts.value: Premature physeal closure after distal tibial physeal fracture: 12.1%; distal ulna: 19.6% growth disturbance; physeal bars after Salter-Harris III or IV medial malleolus fractures: 30.4%

grading: Salter–Harris classification (types I–V)

structures: Epiphysis and articular surface (types III and IV)
differentials: Distal radius fracture (torus or other pattern)
Little League shoulder or elbow (physeal stress)
keywords.mechanism: In a growing child the physis is the weakest part of the long bone, weaker than the ligaments and the adjacent bone, so forces that sprain a ligament or break the bone in an adult can instead split the growth plate (standard anatomical teaching). The commonest mechanism is a fall: the child trips, reaches out and lands on an outstretched hand, loading the distal radius physis in compression, bending and shear, which gives a Salter–Harris II fracture of the distal radius in most cases [r4]. At the ankle the pattern depends on the position of the foot at injury, for example supination and plantar flexion in 33.6% of ankle physeal fractures [r9,r13]. The fracture line follows the physis and then exits through the metaphysis (type II), the epiphysis to the joint (type III) or both (type IV) [r14,r2].

name: Plantar heel pain (plantar fasciopathy)
populations: runners and other physically active adults
people with a higher body mass index
people who stand or walk for long periods
adults with limited ankle dorsiflexion or first MTP extension
summary: A load-related degenerative condition of the plantar fascia at the medial calcaneal tubercle. It causes first-step heel pain that eases with warming up and is managed with education, load control and strengthening.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Often slow: in one hospital cohort 54% were asymptomatic at a mean of 9.7 years, and 50% still had the condition at 5 years

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based and gradual (no validated criteria): pain-controlled loaded single-leg calf work first, then a graded walk–run program

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: First-step pain plus focal tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle. Weight-bearing windlass test: sensitivity 31.8%, specificity 100% in one small study

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose. Ultrasound shows a thickened fascia (about 6.7–6.9 mm at baseline in one cohort), but thickness did not predict prognosis

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Estimated to affect 7–10% of the population

keyFacts.label: Key treatment
keyFacts.value: High-load heel raises beat plantar-specific stretching at 3 months (Foot Function Index 29 points lower), but groups were equal by 6 and 12 months

tests: Palpation of the medial calcaneal tubercle
Tinel's test over the tarsal tunnel and Baxter's nerve
structures: Abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis
differentials: Heel fat pad syndrome or contusion
Baxter's nerve entrapment or tarsal tunnel syndrome
keywords.mechanism: Plantar heel pain has no single injury moment. It develops from thousands of loaded steps a day that repeatedly tension the plantar fascia. The fascia is stretched as the arch lowers in early stance, then tightened by the windlass mechanism as the heel lifts and the great toe extends at the first MTP joint, so tensile load is transmitted to its calcaneal enthesis [r5]. When load rises faster than the fascia's capacity to adapt, the tissue at the origin changes structure and becomes painful [r4,r1].

name: Posterior ankle impingement
populations: people with an os trigonum or a prominent lateral talar process
summary: Posterior ankle pain in forced plantarflexion as the posterior talar process or os trigonum, capsule and soft tissue are squeezed between the tibia and calcaneus, typical in dancers and footballers.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Forced or repeated plantarflexion: en pointe or demi-pointe, kicking, push-off, downhill running

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve with non-surgical care; in one small series 60% improved without surgery and 40% needed excision

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior pain reproduced by forced passive plantarflexion; diagnosis is mainly clinical

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral radiograph in maximal plantarflexion shows an os trigonum or posterior process; MRI shows soft tissue and oedema

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. Full activity after arthroscopic excision averaged 11.3 weeks versus 16.0 weeks after open surgery

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No population estimate found; dance accounts for 62% of sports cases reported in one review

grading: Descriptive classification by dominant pathology (no validated grading)

tests: Forced passive plantarflexion test (posterior impingement test)
Resisted great-toe flexion with the ankle plantarflexed (FHL test)
structures: Posterior talar process (lateral tubercle) and os trigonum
Os trigonum or posterior talar process
differentials: Flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy or tenosynovitis
keywords.mechanism: Forced plantarflexion closes the gap between the back of the tibia and the top of the calcaneus. In dancers en pointe, MRI showed the posterior edge of the tibial plafond, the posterior talus and the superior calcaneus converging in all nine dancers scanned [r7]. The posterior talar process, an os trigonum if present, and the soft tissue behind them are compressed between these bones [r2,r3]. Repeated loading in dancers, footballers and downhill runners, or a single hyperplantarflexion or inversion–plantarflexion injury, produces pain, swelling and sometimes fracture [r5,r1].

name: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury
populations: motor vehicle and motorcycle trauma patients
summary: A partial or complete tear of the PCL from a posteriorly directed force on the proximal tibia with the knee flexed, such as a dashboard impact or a fall onto a bent knee with the foot pointed.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Isolated grade I–II: timing varies and is criteria-based (often weeks to a few months); reconstruction 9–12 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Dashboard impact (~35%) or fall on the flexed knee with foot plantarflexed (~24%)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior drawer with tibial step-off (Sn 90%, Sp 99% in chronic isolated tears)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI for acute injury; posterior stress radiographs quantify laxity (>8 mm suggests complete tear, >12 mm combined injury)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mid-20s to early 30s

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Up to 38% of acute knee haemarthroses in trauma centres; mostly combined injuries

grading: Clinical grading of posterior laxity (posterior drawer at 90° flexion, tibial step-off)

tests: Dial test (tibial external rotation) at 30° and 90°
structures: Posterior cruciate ligament (anterolateral and posteromedial bundles)
Posterolateral corner (LCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament)
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a posteriorly directed force on the anterior proximal tibia while the knee is flexed to about 90°. This happens when the tibia strikes the dashboard in a car crash, or when an athlete falls forward onto a flexed knee with the ankle plantarflexed so that the tibial tuberosity, rather than the patella, takes the impact [r3]. The tibia is driven backward in the sagittal plane and the PCL, which is tight in flexion, fails. Hyperflexion and hyperextension are less common mechanisms; hyperextension and varus-rotation mechanisms often injure the posterolateral corner as well [r1].

name: Posterior shoulder dislocation and instability
populations: people with epilepsy or after electric shock
summary: The humeral head slips or dislocates backward from axial load on a flexed, adducted arm, a seizure or shock, or repeated microtrauma. Locked dislocations are often missed; recurrent cases start with rehabilitation.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation of at least 6 months for recurrent subluxation; after arthroscopic stabilisation, return to play took 4.3 to 8.6 months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: After arthroscopic stabilisation 86.4% returned to play and 68.0% to the same or higher level

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Kim test (sensitivity 80%, specificity 94%) and jerk test (73%, 98%) in one study of 172 painful shoulders; combined sensitivity 97%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: A locked dislocation can look normal on an AP film: obtain an axillary or scapular Y view, then CT. MRI arthrography for the labrum; CT for bone loss

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young men: 83.3% male and mean age 26.1 years in arthroscopic stabilisation series; fracture-dislocations 35–55 years

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 10% of shoulder instability; acute traumatic posterior dislocation 1.1 per 100,000 person-years, about 20 times rarer than anterior

grading: Descriptive patterns (no validated grading)

differentials: Internal impingement in the overhead athlete
keywords.mechanism: The shoulder is driven backward when force passes along the humerus through a flexed, adducted and internally rotated arm, for example a fall onto the hand, a lineman's block, a press-up or a bench press. In a seizure, electric shock or electroconvulsive therapy, the internal rotators contract violently and overpower the external rotators, so the head is forced out backward [r3]. Repeated sub-injury loads in the same position injure the posteroinferior capsule and labrum without a single event [r4,r1].

name: Posterolateral corner (LCL/PLC) injury
summary: Injury to the lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament from a varus, hyperextension or external rotation force. Usually combined with cruciate injury; easily missed.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Varus stress at 0° and 30°; dial test at 30° and 90°

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI; varus stress radiographs (>4 mm side-to-side suggests grade III)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 9.1% of acute knee haemarthroses; 87% are combined injuries

keyFacts.label: Nerve risk
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about one in four operated PLC injuries

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I–II: 6–12 weeks; grade III reconstruction: 9–12 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Blow to the anteromedial knee in extension (hyperextension–varus)

grading: Clinical grading of varus/rotational laxity (with varus stress radiographs)

tests: Dial test (tibial external rotation at 30° and 90°)
structures: Medial femoral condyle and tibial plateau
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a posterolaterally directed blow to the anteromedial proximal tibia with the knee in or near full extension, which forces hyperextension and varus [r3]. Non-contact hyperextension–varus (landing or stepping awkwardly), and forced external rotation of the tibia on a flexed knee, also cause PLC injury. The force opens the lateral compartment in the frontal plane while the tibia rotates externally, and the medial compartment is compressed: an anteromedial femoral condyle bone bruise is a common MRI marker of this mechanism [r6].

name: Prepatellar bursitis
populations: tradespeople who kneel (tilers, carpet and floor layers, plumbers)
summary: Inflammation and swelling of the bursa in front of the kneecap from repeated kneeling, a blow or infection. About a third of cases are septic and need aspiration-guided antibiotic treatment.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: At least 10 per 100,000 per year (with olecranon bursitis); 80% male, aged 40–60

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive kneeling, a direct blow or fall onto the patella, or skin breach

keyFacts.label: Septic
keyFacts.value: About one-third of cases; Staphylococcus aureus causes about 80%

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Bursal aspirate (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals) separates septic from non-septic

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound confirms a bursal collection and helps distinguish cellulitis

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Non-septic: 2–6 weeks with protection from kneeling

grading: Aetiological classification

keywords.mechanism: The bursa is compressed between the floor and the patella with every kneel, and shear between skin and bone irritates its synovial lining. Repeated microtrauma (chronic kneeling) provokes inflammation and fluid production. A direct blow causes bleeding into the bursa (haemorrhagic bursitis). Because the bursa lies just under the skin, an abrasion or puncture can introduce bacteria, usually Staphylococcus aureus, causing septic bursitis [r1,r6].

name: Proximal (long head) biceps rupture
aka: ruptured biceps tendon at the shoulder
populations: people with rotator cuff tendinopathy or tears
manual workers who lift heavy loads
summary: Rupture of the long head of biceps at the shoulder, usually in an older or tendinopathic tendon, with a pop, bruising and a 'Popeye' bulge. Most people do well without surgery, with a modest loss of strength.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Pain and bruising settle over weeks (clinical convention); the muscle bulge is permanent without surgery

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; commonly about 3 months after non-operative care once pain and strength allow, longer after tenodesis (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Inspection for a Popeye deformity with resisted elbow flexion, plus a cuff examination; Speed's and Yergason's tests add little

keyFacts.label: Strength loss without surgery
keyFacts.value: In a small old isokinetic series, elbow flexion fell by 16% and supination by 11% (10 patients); a review quotes 8–21%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound is highly specific for complete rupture (LR+ 35.50); MRI specificity is 93.0%–99.0%

keyFacts.label: Proportion proximal
keyFacts.value: About 3% of all biceps tendon ruptures are distal, so most are proximal

tests: Inspection for Popeye deformity with resisted elbow flexion
Hook test and biceps squeeze test (distal biceps)
structures: Short head of biceps and coracoid origin
Bicipital groove, transverse humeral ligament and sheath
Distal biceps tendon at the radial tuberosity
differentials: Muscle strain or haematoma of the biceps
keywords.mechanism: The tendon usually fails in an older or already degenerate segment under a load that would not injure a healthy tendon: typically a sudden forceful contraction or an unexpected pull while the biceps is working eccentrically, such as lifting or catching a heavy object (clinical observation) [r2,r3]. The rupture usually occurs inside the joint close to its origin at the labrum [r7], and the muscle then retracts toward the elbow, producing the Popeye bulge.

name: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy
populations: people who sit for long periods on hard seats
summary: A persistent, load-related pain at the hamstring origin on the ischial tuberosity. Running, hard-surface sitting and deep hip flexion provoke it, and management is education plus progressive tendon loading.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months rather than weeks. Strength recovery can take 3–6 months or more in long-standing cases

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-monitoring rules, strength at least equal to the other side, and graded running and hip-flexion exposure

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Localised ischial pain with pain-provocation tests (Puranen-Orava, bent-knee stretch, modified bent-knee stretch); good inter-examiner reliability, validity moderate to high

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis. MRI or ultrasound can support it or exclude a tear, avulsion or bone injury

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: No reliable data. It affects athletic and non-athletic adults

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Not well established. Prevalence data are sparse, although it is reported as common in runners

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, to be read alongside pain and function [r3,r4]

structures: Biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus
Gluteus maximus, adductor magnus and triceps surae
differentials: Stress reaction or fracture of the ischium or pubic ramus
keywords.mechanism: PHT has no single injury event. It develops when the demands on the common hamstring tendon exceed its capacity. Two kinds of load act at the ischial tuberosity: tensile load from hamstring contraction, mainly in running, and compressive load from higher ranges of hip flexion or from direct pressure in sitting [r2,r3]. On surgical and imaging studies the tendinopathic change lies next to the tendon's insertion on the ischial tuberosity, which supports compression as a contributing factor [r2]. Tendinopathic tendons are thought to tolerate compression poorly because the tendon swells and its matrix changes [r2].

name: Proximal hamstring tendon avulsion
populations: middle-aged and older women injured during daily activities
summary: Detachment of one or more hamstring tendons from the ischial tuberosity, usually from forced hip flexion with the knee extended, such as a slip into the splits or a water-skiing fall.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean 49 years; 56% aged 45–59 in a surgical series

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Forced hip flexion with the knee extended against an eccentric hamstring contraction

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI: number of tendons involved, retraction distance and sciatic nerve relationship

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ischial tenderness, palpable gap with the knee flexed, marked knee flexion weakness

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 93.8% after repair, mean 5.7 months

keyFacts.label: Treatment
keyFacts.value: Shared decision: repair or structured non-operative rehab (non-inferior in 30–70-year-olds)

grading: Wood classification of proximal hamstring injuries

tests: Palpable gap / loss of tension test
keywords.mechanism: The hamstrings are loaded eccentrically at their longest: the hip is forced into flexion while the knee stays extended. This happens when the leading foot slips forward, when a water-skier is pulled forward over straight legs (water-skiing was the most frequent cause in one series [r1]), or during an extreme splits-type stretch [r6]. Force concentrates at the tendon–bone junction and the conjoint tendon (biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus), often with semimembranosus, pulls off the ischial tuberosity. The tendons may then retract distally [r2].

name: Proximal humerus fracture
aka: fractured upper arm at the shoulder
populations: older adults, mostly women aged 60 years or over
people with osteoporosis or a high falls risk
summary: A fracture of the upper end of the humerus, most often from a low-energy fall in an older adult. Most heal without surgery, and trials show that surgery for displaced fractures gives no better function than a sling.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most function returns by about 6 months and is maintained to 5 years: in operated PROFHER participants the mean Oxford Shoulder Score was 35.8 at 6 months and 40.1 at 5 years

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mostly an older adult injury, so return to function is the goal; commonly 3 to 6 months for daily and light tasks, longer for heavy tasks (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Radiograph series (AP, scapular Y, axillary) with a neurovascular examination; classify by Neer's parts

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Plain radiographs for diagnosis and Neer classification; CT for complex fractures or surgical planning (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mostly women aged 60 or over (47 trials, 3179 participants in the Cochrane review); mean age 66 and 77% female in PROFHER

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 4% to 5% of all fractures; about 40% are displaced fractures involving the surgical neck

grading: Neer classification (by number of displaced parts), with fracture-dislocation and head-splitting variants

tests: Palpation for bony tenderness and crepitus
Axillary nerve sensation and deltoid isometric contraction test
Neurovascular examination of the arm and hand
structures: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex vessels
Long head of biceps tendon and bicipital groove
Rotator cuff tendons and attached tuberosity fragments
keywords.mechanism: The usual mechanism is a low-energy fall from standing height onto the side of the shoulder or onto the outstretched arm in a person with fragile bone [r2]. Force is transmitted through the humerus and the proximal end fails at the surgical neck or the tuberosities, where the cortex is thin. The cuff muscles then pull the fragments apart, and the displacement pattern defines the Neer type [r4]. In younger people the same fracture usually follows high-energy trauma and is more complex [r3].

name: Pubic-related groin pain (osteitis pubis)
summary: Longstanding groin pain from the pubic symphysis and adjacent pubic bone, best understood as a bone stress response to repetitive shear, with local symphyseal tenderness and often pubic bone marrow oedema on MRI.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Often 3–6 months; slower than other groin entities

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 89% returned the next season after 12 weeks' unloading, but only 41% were symptom-free

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Local tenderness of the pubic symphysis and immediately adjacent bone

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI: pubic bone marrow oedema (also common in pain-free footballers)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Least common Doha entity in a groin clinic (4%)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive shear across the symphysis from kicking, running and cutting

tests: Single-leg hop / single-leg stance pain test
structures: Adductor longus and rectus abdominis entheses
keywords.mechanism: The pubic symphysis transmits load between the two halves of the pelvis. In single-leg stance during running and kicking, the stance-side pubis is driven upward by ground-reaction force while the swing side drops, creating vertical shear and rotation across the symphysis. At the same time the adductors pull the pubic bodies downward and laterally, and the rectus abdominis pulls them upward [r8]. Repetitive cyclical load without adequate recovery produces a bone stress response in the subchondral pubic bone (marrow oedema) and degeneration of the symphyseal disc and margins [r3,r9].

name: Pulled elbow (radial head subluxation)
aka: subluxation of the radial head in children
populations: toddlers and preschool children (about 1 to 4 years)
children held or lifted by the hand
infants who roll over onto an arm
summary: A young child's radial head slips through the annular ligament after a pull on the extended, pronated arm. The child stops using the arm, with no swelling. A quick reduction usually restores function.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Function usually returns within minutes of a successful reduction (one trial re-checked every 5 minutes); hyperpronation failed at the first attempt in 9.2% versus 26.4% with supination-flexion in a Cochrane review (low-quality evidence)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Not applicable in this age group: normal play resumes as soon as the child uses the arm freely (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Clinical diagnosis from a typical history and an arm held still without swelling or bony tenderness; ultrasound with a displaced annular ligament had sensitivity 64.9% and specificity 100% in one study

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs are usually not needed with a typical history, but 5 of 90 children with a clinical diagnosis in one trial had a fracture, so image if the history is atypical, there is swelling or tenderness, or reduction fails

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: In a series of 2331 cases, frequency peaked at 6 months and 2 years; mean age 3.8 years in an ultrasound series

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: The most common cause of upper limb immobility in infants and preschool children at paediatric emergency departments; 2331 cases at one hospital in 10 years

grading: Ultrasound classification of pulled elbow (type I and type II)

tests: Clinical diagnosis: typical history and examination
Return of arm use after a reduction manoeuvre
Ultrasound for a torn annular ligament
keywords.mechanism: Pulled elbow is caused by a sudden pull on the extended, pronated forearm, which draws the radius distally through the annular ligament and subluxates the radial head [r1]. The pull is usually by an adult or taller person, but a fall or twist can do the same [r2]. In an ultrasound series the annular ligament was most often intact but interposed, and in a minority it was torn [r1]. The child cries, then guards the arm and will not use it, with no swelling [r1].

name: Quadriceps (rectus femoris) strain
populations: elite male and female football players
athletes returning after ACL reconstruction with a patellar tendon graft
summary: A tear of the rectus femoris, the two-joint quadriceps muscle, usually from kicking or sprint acceleration, most often near its central tendon or musculotendinous junction in the proximal to mid anterior thigh.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Days to weeks. Mean 20 days to return to full training in elite track and field; central tendon involvement is slower

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free palpation and resisted tests, strength, sprinting and kicking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Localised anterior thigh tenderness with pain on resisted knee extension and hip flexion; a palpable gap suggests a tendon injury

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI at 24–72 h grades the injury and shows central tendon involvement, which predicts a longer rehabilitation

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive kicking and sprinting; the kicking leg is at higher risk

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 19% of muscle injuries in male professional footballers; 11% of all injuries in elite women's football

grading: British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC), based on MRI [r14]

tests: Palpation of the rectus femoris and its tendons
Resisted knee extension and hip flexion
differentials: Rectus femoris proximal tendinopathy or tear
keywords.mechanism: Quadriceps strains occur in sports that involve repetitive kicking and sprinting [r1]. The rectus femoris is the only biarticular quadriceps muscle: it flexes the hip and extends the knee, so it is lengthened by hip extension combined with knee flexion, as in the back-swing of a kick (mechanism reasoning). In a kick, the lengthened muscle then contracts forcefully to drive hip flexion and knee extension through ball contact. The tear is most often near the central tendon or MTJ in the proximal to mid belly [r2,r4].

name: Quadriceps contusion and myositis ossificans
populations: people with a previous quadriceps injury
summary: A direct blow that bleeds into the quadriceps, graded by knee flexion at 12–24 hours. Early knee flexion limits bleeding. Myositis ossificans and, rarely, compartment syndrome are the main complications.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean disability 13, 19 and 21 days for mild, moderate and severe contusions in 117 West Point cadets; mean lay-off 7 days for direct thigh injuries in elite football

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: When pain-free knee flexion and quadriceps size and firmness equal the other side. After immediate flexion to 120° for 24 hours, 47 midshipmen returned at a mean of 3.5 days (uncontrolled series)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Passive knee flexion at 12–24 hours: mild above 90°, moderate 45–90°, severe below 45°

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Often none is needed. Use ultrasound or MRI to define the haematoma, and radiographs or CT if a firm mass or lost flexion persists, for myositis ossificans

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young, active contact-sport athletes. The main series are cadets and midshipmen; direct injuries were 12% of thigh muscle injuries in elite football

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Direct thigh muscle injuries: 0.19 per 1,000 hours in elite football, against 1.48 for indirect injuries. Myositis ossificans developed in 9% of cadets with contusions

grading: Jackson–Feagin grading by passive knee flexion 12–24 hours after injury (thresholds as applied in the West Point cohort) [r4,r5]

tests: Passive knee flexion range (prone) at 12–24 hours
Straight-leg raise with pain-free isometric quadriceps contraction
structures: Fascia lata and anterior thigh compartment
Quadriceps muscle belly (vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, rectus femoris)
differentials: Acute compartment syndrome of the thigh
Femoral shaft fracture or stress injury
Myositis ossificans versus a soft-tissue sarcoma
keywords.mechanism: A contusion follows a direct blunt force to the front or side of the thigh, typically a knee, shoulder, helmet or boot in collision sport, which crushes the quadriceps against the femur. Severity depends on the site of impact, the activation status of the muscle, the age of the patient and fatigue [r1]. The injury is a sequence of microscopic rupture of muscle cells, macroscopic defects in the muscle belly, infiltrative bleeding and inflammation [r2]. The vastus intermedius and vastus lateralis lie closest to the bone, and the knee loses flexion because the swollen, bleeding quadriceps cannot lengthen [r5].

name: Quadriceps tendon rupture
populations: people with diabetes, gout or chronic kidney disease
summary: A sudden failure of the quadriceps tendon just above the patella, usually in people over 40 with a degenerate tendon. Inability to lift the straight leg needs urgent referral, because delayed repair gives poorer results.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: About 3 months to clinical and functional recovery in a small prospective repair series; protecting the repair for about 6 weeks is common

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Systematic review of 378 quadriceps repairs: 89.8% returned to play and 70.0% to the same level (professional athletes 70.9%)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Inability to straight-leg raise or an extensor lag, with a suprapatellar gap. The full triad of pain, impaired extension and a gap was present in only 58.3% of reported bilateral cases

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Plain radiograph first; ultrasound or MRI when the examination is equivocal. Advanced imaging is often unnecessary when the functional deficit is clear

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Over 40 years; mean age 57 (range 16–85) in a systematic review of repairs. Most patients are male

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 1.37 per 100,000 (patellar tendon rupture 0.68 per 100,000)

grading: No validated grading system. Descriptive classification by completeness and timing (clinical convention)

tests: Straight-leg raise and extensor lag test
differentials: Femoral nerve palsy or lumbar radiculopathy
keywords.mechanism: Quadriceps tendon rupture is usually an indirect injury. The quadriceps contracts forcefully, often eccentrically, to stop a flexed knee collapsing under load, for example in a stumble, a missed step or an awkward landing, and the load exceeds what a degenerate tendon can bear [r3,r12]. The tear usually lies at or just above the superior pole of the patella [r5]. In a video analysis of professional-athlete extensor mechanism ruptures (20 patellar and 8 quadriceps), the knee was typically flexed with the ankle plantarflexed and a tendency to valgus at the moment of injury [r15].

name: Radial head fracture
aka: elbow fracture after fall on outstretched hand
radial head fracture (Mason type I to IV)
populations: people in road crashes or falls from height
summary: Fracture of the radial head after a fall on the outstretched hand, causing lateral elbow pain and painful forearm rotation. Most isolated, stable fractures heal well with a sling and early movement.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Isolated stable Mason I–II fractures treated non-operatively: mean DASH 5.8 at about 10 years, with 14% reporting stiffness and 24% some pain (100 patients)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; often about 6–12 weeks for a non-operatively managed stable fracture and longer after surgery (clinical convention; no validated criteria found)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Elbow extension test: sensitivity 96.8% and specificity 48.5% for any elbow fracture in a multicentre study of 1740 eligible adults and children; inability to extend fully means radiographs are needed

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral radiograph at 90° of flexion for the posterior fat pad sign; with an effusion and no visible fracture, 15 of 20 adults (75%) had an occult fracture on MRI, mostly in the radial head

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Median age 43 years (range 13–94), with no sex predominance; women commonly injured in low-energy falls

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: The most common elbow fracture in adults, about one-third of elbow fractures in one review; 199 radial head fractures in a 6872-patient trauma database over a year

grading: Mason classification (original 1954 types I–III, with the commonly added modified type IV)

tests: Posterior fat pad (and anterior fat pad) sign on a lateral radiograph
Forearm rotation and radial head palpation
Wrist, distal radioulnar joint and interosseous membrane screen
Valgus and varus stress and posterolateral rotatory stability testing (when pain allows)
structures: Interosseous membrane and distal radioulnar joint
differentials: Capitellum, coronoid, olecranon or distal humerus fracture
keywords.mechanism: In the usual mechanism the person falls onto the outstretched hand and an axial load travels up the forearm, driving the radial head into the capitellum (standard mechanism; it is not measured in the sources reviewed). The radial head is the lateral column of the elbow, so a high-energy or rotational version of the same fall may also dislocate the elbow or tear the collateral ligaments. Fracture type depends on the load, the forearm rotation at impact and bone quality. Women commonly sustain these in low-energy falls [r2]. Mason described the original three fracture types by displacement and comminution [r1, r3].

name: Rotator cuff related shoulder pain (subacromial pain)
populations: people returning to activity after a lay-off
summary: Activity-related shoulder pain with a painful arc, from load exceeding the capacity of the rotator cuff tendons. 'Impingement' as a purely mechanical explanation is contested.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Usually months of progressive loading; symptoms can persist or recur

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, commonly about 3–6 months for overhead athletes (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Cluster of findings: painful arc, pain on resisted tests, Hawkins–Kennedy and Neer (no single test is diagnostic)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine; ultrasound if no improvement after about 6 weeks or a full-thickness tear is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: About 50 years (peak consultation incidence for shoulder conditions)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 1.47% of UK adults consult yearly for any shoulder condition

tests: External rotation lag sign and drop-arm sign
structures: Supraspinatus tendon (critical zone near the footprint)
differentials: Internal impingement in the overhead athlete
keywords.mechanism: RCRSP usually develops gradually when the demands placed on the cuff tendons and subacromial tissues exceed their capacity, often after a change in overhead activity, a period of inactivity or a minor strain. Pain is typically provoked during loaded elevation, classically between about 60° and 120° of abduction (the painful arc, a clinical convention). The idea that the tendon is squeezed beneath the acromion is contested [r3,r1].

name: Sacroiliac joint pain
populations: adults with chronic non-radicular low back pain
summary: A contested source of unilateral low back and buttock pain thought to arise from the sacroiliac joint or its ligaments. Diagnosis rests on a cluster of provocation tests, and the treatment evidence is mixed.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Estimated at 15–30% of chronic non-radicular low back pain in one review; the estimate is contested because no true gold standard exists

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Three or more of six provocation tests positive: sensitivity 94%, specificity 78% against an anaesthetic block (48 patients); single tests are uninformative

keyFacts.label: Pain pattern
keyFacts.value: Unilateral pain below L5, but referral varies widely; injecting the joint in pain-free volunteers produced pain about 10 cm below and 3 cm lateral to the PSIS

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: No imaging finding confirms a painful sacroiliac joint; imaging excludes other causes such as sacroiliitis, fracture or tumour

keyFacts.label: Treatment evidence
keyFacts.value: Mixed: manual therapy 72%, intra-articular steroid 50% and physiotherapy 20% success in a 51-patient trial; radiofrequency gave no clinically important benefit over exercise in the Mint trial

keyFacts.label: Red flag
keyFacts.value: Fever, severe pain with inability to weight-bear, night pain, inflammatory back pain or neurological or sphincter change need medical review

tests: Cluster of SIJ pain provocation tests (three or more positive of six)
Three or more positive stressing tests (pooled composite)
Distraction (gapping), sacral thrust and Gaenslen's tests
Standing hip flexion (Gillet) test and other motion tests
structures: Gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, multifidus and thoracolumbar fascia
differentials: Hip joint pathology (femoroacetabular impingement, labral tear, osteoarthritis)
keywords.mechanism: No single mechanism is established. The sacroiliac joint transfers load between the spine and the legs [r11], and pain is attributed to loading that exceeds the capacity of the joint capsule and ligaments: a sudden jolt or fall, repeated asymmetrical loading, or altered load transfer after pregnancy, spinal surgery or leg length difference [r1]. The joint moves very little: radiostereometric measurement in 22 patients with SIJ pain found very small movements, so the idea of a joint 'out of place' is not well supported [r12].

name: Scaphoid fracture
populations: athletes in contact and ball sports
people after a fall on an outstretched hand
summary: A break of the scaphoid, usually at the waist, from a fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist extended and radially deviated. Snuffbox tenderness needs imaging, as missed fractures risk nonunion and AVN.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Cast immobilisation for undisplaced waist fractures, then rehabilitation; trial outcomes are measured at 52 weeks (SWIFFT)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Snuffbox tenderness is sensitive (0.87–1.00 across studies) but not specific (0.03–0.98); combining tests raises specificity

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs can miss fractures; in a meta-analysis MRI had sensitivity 94.2% and specificity 97.7%, CT 81.5% and 96.0%

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adults; mean age 33 and 83% men in the SWIFFT trial

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 29 per 100,000 per year in a one-year Edinburgh study of radiographically confirmed fractures

keyFacts.label: Key risk
keyFacts.value: Blood enters the scaphoid mainly at the distal end, so proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis and nonunion

grading: Herbert classification (clinical convention) with a displacement threshold of 2 mm

structures: Scaphoid waist (most commonly) and proximal pole
Scapholunate ligament and other carpal ligaments
Soft tissues and radial wrist tendons
differentials: Thumb ulnar collateral ligament injury (skier's thumb)
keywords.mechanism: Most scaphoid fractures follow a fall on an outstretched hand in which the wrist is forced into extension and radial deviation. The scaphoid, which spans the proximal and distal carpal rows, is compressed between the radius and the distal row and then bent over the radial styloid. It fails at its narrowest part, the waist, and the fracture line usually runs obliquely or transversely across the bone (clinical biomechanics). The commonest pattern in a prospective series was a complete waist fracture [r2].

name: Scapholunate ligament injury
populations: adults after a fall on the outstretched hand
athletes in falls and contact sports
people with persisting dorsal wrist pain after a wrist sprain
adults with an associated distal radius or scaphoid injury
summary: Tear of the scapholunate interosseous ligament after a fall on the extended wrist, causing dorsal wrist pain and carpal instability. Missed injuries can progress to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) arthritis.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Scaphoid shift (Watson) test: described as helpful for scaphoid stability, but accuracy figures were not retrieved. A newer SL C-sign had sensitivity 86% and specificity 83% in 28 patients

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Clenched-fist stress view: sensitivity 40% and specificity 82% against arthroscopy (124 patients); a normal stress view does not exclude a Geissler grade 3 or higher tear

keyFacts.label: Reference standard
keyFacts.value: Wrist arthroscopy. A negative MRI cannot rule out an SL ligament injury (negative predictive value 72–94% across studies)

keyFacts.label: Treatment evidence
keyFacts.value: No trial compares repair, reconstruction and conservative care. Reviews of chronic tears found no technique clearly superior; pain fell from 6.0 to 2.8 at 2 years across techniques

keyFacts.label: Timing
keyFacts.value: Chronic after about 6 weeks, when ligament healing is no longer considered possible, so a persisting wrist sprain should be reassessed early

keyFacts.label: Natural history
keyFacts.value: An untreated SL injury can progress to SLAC wrist, but the rate of progression was not quantified in the sources retrieved

grading: Mayfield stages of perilunar instability, with the arthroscopic Geissler grade and the Watson SLAC stages used for SL tears and their sequel. Stage details beyond those quoted follow the classic schemes

tests: Dorsal SL palpation and loaded-extension pain
structures: Extrinsic palmar and dorsal carpal ligaments
Flexor carpi radialis and radial wrist extensors
differentials: Perilunate dislocation or lunate dislocation (Mayfield stages II–IV)
Dorsal wrist ganglion, extensor tendinopathy or Kienböck's disease
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a fall on the outstretched hand with the wrist extended, ulnar deviated and the carpus in intercarpal supination. In cadaver loading studies this combination produced sequential ligament failure, starting with the scapholunate ligament (stage I perilunar instability) and progressing to lunate dislocation (stage IV) [r3]. Smaller loads may tear only part of the SL ligament and leave a wrist that is stable at rest but unstable under load (dynamic instability) [r1,r6].

name: Sinding-Larsen–Johansson syndrome
summary: A traction apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella in active adolescents. It causes activity-related pain at the lower kneecap and usually settles with load modification, though the evidence is limited.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Uncommon: about 0.8% of 12–15-year-olds had MRI features in one cohort; quoted rates of 2–5% come from a case report

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mainly physically active adolescents aged 9–17 years, more often boys

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella with a normal straight-leg raise; no validated test accuracy data

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs may be normal early; ultrasound or MRI is the most useful. Exclude patellar sleeve fracture

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Conservative care reported to give positive outcomes within about 2–8 months; evidence is mostly case reports

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Education, load management and progressive exercise (extrapolated from Osgood–Schlatter disease)

tests: Palpation of the inferior pole of the patella
differentials: Bipartite patella or other normal variant
keywords.mechanism: SLJ is a traction injury. Repeated quadriceps contraction in jumping, running and kicking pulls the patella proximally, and the patellar tendon holds the inferior pole of the patella. The tendon attachment on the growing inferior pole is the weak link, so the tendon is loaded at its proximal attachment, which can be partially avulsed, with de novo calcification [r1]. The condition is attributed to repeated microtrauma [r10]. It usually lacks a single injury event, although an acute presentation after a non-contact jump or kick has been reported [r11,r5].

name: Skier's / gamekeeper's thumb (thumb UCL injury)
summary: A valgus-abduction force at the thumb MCP joint tears the ulnar collateral ligament, usually at its distal attachment. A Stener lesion will not heal in a cast and usually needs surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Partial tears: nonoperative care usually favoured. Complete tears: surgery recommended; athletes returned to sport within 5–8 weeks of surgery in a review (up to 98.1%)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Valgus stress at 0° and 30° of MCP flexion: no firm endpoint suggests a complete tear

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound for a Stener lesion: pooled sensitivity 96% and specificity 90% (17 studies); MRI 93% and 98% in a separate meta-analysis

keyFacts.label: Stener lesion
keyFacts.value: 51.4% of 35 surgically treated soldiers had one; 95% of 262 hand surgeons favour surgery for it

keyFacts.label: Skiing context
keyFacts.value: Isolated UCL lesions were 16.9% of 195 distal upper limb ski injuries in one two-season study

keyFacts.label: Evidence quality
keyFacts.value: No randomised trials of operative versus nonoperative care were found; evidence is cohorts, reviews and surveys

grading: Clinical grading by laxity and endpoint, with the Stener lesion and avulsion fracture as modifiers

tests: Valgus stress test at 0° and 30° of MCP flexion
Ultrasound for a Stener lesion (imaging test)
differentials: Thumb MCP radial collateral ligament injury
Thumb MCP dislocation or volar plate injury
Thumb CMC joint sprain or osteoarthritis
keywords.mechanism: The classic injury is a fall onto an outstretched hand with the thumb abducted, often with the ski pole handle gripped, so that the handle or the ground levers the thumb into valgus (abduction) at the MCP joint [r10,r3]. The UCL is loaded beyond its capacity and fails, usually at its distal attachment on the proximal phalanx [r4]. Forced abduction or hyperextension are the recognised mechanisms [r2].

name: SLAP lesion (superior labral tear)
populations: adults of working and athletic age
older adults (often an incidental imaging finding)
summary: A tear of the superior labrum around the biceps anchor, from throwing peel-back, traction or a fall onto the arm. Labral findings are common without symptoms, so rehabilitation comes first and surgery is contested.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation first: athletes who completed non-operative rehabilitation had about 20 physiotherapy sessions, and return to play was generally within 6 months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Non-operative care: 78% returned to play if they completed rehabilitation (53.7% overall); return to prior performance 72% in completers (42.6% overall)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test is accurate alone. Biceps Load II had LR+ 1.7 and LR- 0.39 in one study; compression–rotation had the best pooled LR+ (2.81)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI or MR arthrography, read with caution: superior labral tears were reported on MRI in 55% and 72% of asymptomatic 45–60-year-olds (two readers)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Working and athletic adults: mean age 37.5 years in the original series and 40 years in the sham-controlled trial

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 6% to 26% of shoulder arthroscopies; US diagnosis rate rose from 28.0 to 142.4 per 100,000 between 2003 and 2013

grading: Snyder classification (types I–IV), with the Morgan subtypes of type II and later combined patterns (Maffet and others)

structures: Long head of biceps tendon and its anchor
differentials: Internal impingement in the overhead athlete
keywords.mechanism: Three mechanisms are described. Compression is a fall onto the outstretched arm with the shoulder abducted and slightly forward flexed, the commonest in the original series [r1]. Traction is a sudden pull on the arm or a forceful biceps contraction that loads the biceps anchor. In throwers, the late-cocking position (about 90° abduction and maximal external rotation) is proposed to produce a torsional peel-back of the posterosuperior labrum by the biceps anchor [r2]. In one series traction accounted for 22% of mechanisms, compression 28% and overhead sport 25% [r3].

name: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)
populations: children and adolescents aged about 8–15 years
children with endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, growth hormone treatment)
summary: The femoral head (capital epiphysis) slips off the femoral neck through the growth plate in an adolescent, often presenting as a limp with thigh or knee pain. Same-day referral and non-weight-bearing are needed.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: About 8–15 years, during the adolescent growth spurt

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 10.8 per 100,000 children

keyFacts.label: Key sign
keyFacts.value: Hip held in external rotation as it is flexed, with reduced internal rotation

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Both hips: AP plus frog-leg (stable) or cross-table lateral (unstable) radiographs

keyFacts.label: Stability
keyFacts.value: Unstable slips (cannot bear weight) had 47% AVN vs 0% in stable slips

keyFacts.label: Pitfall
keyFacts.value: Knee or thigh pain doubles the diagnostic delay; always examine the hip

grading: Loder stability classification (with slip-angle severity)

keywords.mechanism: SCFE is a mechanical failure of the proximal femoral physis under shear. During the growth spurt the physis is thicker and its hypertrophic zone weaker; excess body weight raises the shear force across it, and a more vertical physis or retroverted femoral neck increases that shear [r1,r10]. The physis gradually gives way (stable slip) or fails suddenly after minor trauma (unstable slip). The epiphysis stays in the acetabulum while the neck displaces anteriorly and rotates externally.

name: Spondylolisthesis
populations: adolescent athletes in extension-and-rotation sports (isthmic, usually L5 on S1)
older adults (degenerative, usually L4 on L5)
summary: Forward slip of one lumbar vertebra on the one below: isthmic (pars defect, usually L5 on S1, often adolescent athletes) or degenerative (usually L4 on L5, older adults). Most slips are low grade and benign.

keyFacts.label: Natural history
keyFacts.value: In a 45-year prospective study, unilateral defects never slipped, slip progression slowed each decade and no one reached a 40% slip

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Spondylolysis 5.9% on CT in Japan, 90.3% at L5; a slip was present in 74.5% of bilateral and 7.7% of unilateral defects

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Step-deformity palpation: sensitivity 60–88%, specificity 87–100% for spondylolisthesis in athletes (one low-risk-of-bias study)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Standing lateral radiograph to measure and grade the slip; flexion–extension views for instability; MRI if neural compression is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Isthmic slips begin in childhood or adolescence, most progressing around the growth spurt; degenerative slips occur in older adults

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most low-grade slips are managed without surgery; surgery helps selected people with persistent disabling symptoms (SPORT as-treated analysis)

grading: Meyerding classification (percentage of slip) [r2]

tests: History: pain worse with sitting and walking
Straight leg raise and slump test
structures: Nerve roots (L5 in the L5–S1 foramen; the cauda equina centrally)
Exiting nerve root (L5 in L5–S1 slips)
Central canal and cauda equina (degenerative L4–5 slips)
keywords.mechanism: In the isthmic type, repeated extension and rotation load the pars interarticularis until it fails as a stress fracture. When the defect does not unite on both sides, nothing links the vertebral body to its posterior arch, so the body and the superior part of the arch are free to slide forward on the segment below under anterior shear, most often L5 on S1 [r3]. In the degenerative type there is no pars defect: facet joint osteoarthritis and disc degeneration let the vertebra slip forward, usually at L4–5 (clinical teaching), and facet osteoarthritis was strongly associated with it [r9].

name: Spondylolysis (pars stress fracture)
summary: A fatigue (stress) fracture of the pars interarticularis, most often at L5, from repetitive lumbar extension and rotation in adolescent athletes. Early-stage lesions can heal, so prompt diagnosis matters.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescent athletes: 47% of 100 adolescent athletes with back pain had spondylolysis, versus 5% of adults with acute low back pain

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: 5.9% of the Japanese general population on CT (90% at L5); 8.0% of Spanish elite athletes, up to 26.7% in throwing sports

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No physical test is diagnostic; the one-legged hyperextension test was not supported (sensitivity 50–73%, specificity 0–87%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI found active spondylolysis missed by radiographs in 48.5% of 200 young athletes; SPECT or CT is more sensitive but uses radiation

keyFacts.label: Healing
keyFacts.value: Union with a hard brace: 94% early, 64% and 27% progressive (high and low MRI signal), 0% terminal defects

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
