keyFacts.value: Median 2.5 months (75 days) to return to sport in one 12-athlete functional progression series

grading: CT stage (early, progressive, terminal) with STIR MRI subdivision of progressive defects

differentials: Other bone stress injury or apophyseal ring injury
Infection, tumour or inflammatory back pain
keywords.mechanism: Repetitive lumbar extension combined with rotation, and torsion against resistance, loads the pars interarticularis of the lower lumbar vertebrae, most often L5, until bone microdamage outpaces repair [r1,r4]. The lesion progresses from a bone stress reaction with marrow oedema to an incomplete and then a complete stress fracture; early lesions can heal, while terminal lesions form a non-union [r9,r10].

name: Sport-related concussion
summary: A traumatic brain injury from a blow or impulsive force to the head, causing short-lived neurological impairment. Check red flags first. Imaging is normally normal, and most people recover within weeks.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean 14.0 days to symptom-free (95% CI 12.7–15.4) in a meta-analysis of 278 studies, with very high heterogeneity; most people recover within weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Staged and criteria-based. Mean 19.8 days to return to sport, about twice the 8.3 days to return to school

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Diagnosis is clinical. The SCAT6 is most useful within 72 hours of injury and loses utility by 7 days

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Normally normal. CT is used only to exclude intracranial injury when red flags or a decision rule call for it

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Pooled youth incidence 1.41 per 1000 athlete exposures across 21 sports; highest in taekwondo, rugby union and ice hockey

tests: Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 (SCAT6) and Child SCAT6
Vestibular and Ocular Motor Screening (VOMS) and eye-movement testing
Tandem stance error count (Balance Error Scoring System)
structures: Cerebral cortex and subcortical white matter
Upper cervical spine and neck muscles
Cortex under the impact and at the opposite pole
differentials: Migraine, dehydration, hypoglycaemia, exertional heat illness, cardiac or substance-related causes
keywords.mechanism: Concussion follows a direct blow to the head, or an impulsive force transmitted to the head from a blow to the face, neck or body [r4,r5]. The head accelerates both linearly and in rotation. The brain floats in cerebrospinal fluid, so it lags the skull, strikes the inner table under the impact (coup), then rebounds against the opposite pole (contrecoup). Rotational acceleration also strains the white matter [r13]. The common trigger is a head-to-head, head-to-shoulder or head-to-ground collision.

name: Tibial plateau fracture
summary: An intra-articular fracture of the proximal tibia caused by axial load combined with valgus or varus, from a low-energy fall in older adults or high-energy trauma. Compartment syndrome and soft tissue injury are common.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 10 per 100,000 per year; peaks at 40–60 years

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Schatzker I–VI (lateral split → bicondylar)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ottawa knee rules to trigger radiographs (Sn 0.99)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs then CT for fracture planning; MRI shows soft tissue injury

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Protected weight-bearing 6–12 weeks; return to sport ~7 months or longer

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: About 70% return overall

grading: Schatzker classification

structures: Leg compartments and common peroneal nerve
keywords.mechanism: Most plateau fractures result from an axial load through the extended or slightly flexed knee combined with a valgus (or, less often, varus) force. The femoral condyle acts like a hammer on the plateau below it: valgus drives the lateral femoral condyle into the lateral plateau, splitting the cortex and depressing the articular surface. In dense young bone the plateau tends to split; in osteoporotic bone it tends to depress. Varus loading produces medial plateau fractures, which are often higher energy and may be fracture-dislocations; pure high-energy axial loads produce bicondylar fractures [r2].

name: Tibial stress fracture
populations: female athletes with low energy availability
summary: A fatigue crack in the tibia from cumulative loading beyond the bone's remodelling capacity. Posteromedial lesions usually heal with load management; the anterior mid-shaft is a high-risk site.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Low-risk sites: roughly 6–14 weeks (MRI-graded means 42–99 days across sites). High-risk anterior cortex: months, sometimes surgery

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: bony tenderness resolved, pain-free walking, strength and loading tests passed, and radiological healing at high-risk sites

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal bony tenderness with pain on single-leg hop; percussion pain suggests a more severe lesion

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI is the mainstay. Radiographs were abnormal in only 9.8% of athletes imaged at presentation in a 320-case series

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: The tibia accounted for 49.1% of 320 bone-scan-positive stress fractures in athletes

keyFacts.label: Risk status
keyFacts.value: Anterior mid-shaft cortex is high risk (tension side, relatively avascular): delayed union and non-union can occur

grading: Kaeding and Miller stress fracture classification (grade, location, imaging modality) with site risk [r12,r5]

structures: Tibial cortex at the injury site
keywords.mechanism: A tibial stress fracture develops over weeks, not in one moment. Repetitive running load produces microdamage faster than targeted remodelling can remove it [r1]. Each stride sends an impact load up the tibia at foot contact [r10], and through stance and push-off the shaft bends under ground reaction and calf muscle forces. The anterior mid-shaft is a tension-side site where tensile forces and relative avascularity lead to poor healing [r5].

name: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction
populations: middle-aged and older adults, mostly women
people with a flat or valgus foot
runners and walkers with new medial ankle pain
summary: Progressive overload and degeneration of the tibialis posterior tendon behind the medial malleolus. Without support it can lead to medial arch collapse, now called progressive collapsing foot deformity.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Early stages improve over about 10–12 weeks of exercise with orthoses in small trials; flexible stage II is often managed with long-term bracing

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria. Return to running needs pain-free single-leg heel rise and arch control (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Single heel-rise test, plus palpation behind the medial malleolus and resisted inversion. These signs were negative in 20–35% of confirmed cases in one series

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs for alignment; ultrasound or MRI for the tendon

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Treated series are mostly women, mean age about 58–64 years

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No population incidence found in the sources read

grading: Johnson–Strom stages as modified by Myerson (new PCFD classification proposed but not validated)

tests: Palpation and resisted inversion in plantarflexion
Flexibility of the hindfoot (passive heel correction)
structures: Medial longitudinal arch (talonavicular and naviculocuneiform joints)
differentials: Inflammatory arthritis or subtalar and talonavicular arthritis
keywords.mechanism: PTTD has no single injury moment. Repetitive load on the tibialis posterior tendon, which is the main dynamic supporter of the medial arch and hindfoot, gradually outstrips its capacity. In the continuum model of tendinopathy, a tendon passes from a reactive stage to disrepair and then degeneration, and the later stages have limited capacity to reverse [r9,r10]. As the tendon thickens, elongates or tears, the foot loses support: in PCFD the result is a variable combination of hindfoot valgus, forefoot abduction and midfoot varus [r1]. A congenital valgus calcaneus, forefoot supination or abduction and a short gastrocnemius add to the load [r3].

name: Traumatic hip dislocation
populations: young adult males in road traffic crashes
summary: The femoral head is forced out of the acetabulum, usually posteriorly when a flexed, adducted hip is driven backwards along the femur (dashboard injury). Reduction within 6 hours limits avascular necrosis.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Protected weight-bearing about 6–8 weeks; return to sport often 3–6 months if no AVN

keyFacts.label: Key priority
keyFacts.value: Emergency reduction: AVN risk rises sharply with delay (OR 5.6 if reduced after 12 h)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis, then post-reduction CT; MRI at about 6 weeks to screen for AVN

keyFacts.label: Direction
keyFacts.value: About 90% posterior: leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated

keyFacts.label: Nerve injury
keyFacts.value: About 10% of adults, mainly the sciatic (peroneal division)

keyFacts.label: Long-term
keyFacts.value: AVN and post-traumatic arthritis are common, especially with associated fractures

grading: Thompson–Epstein classification (posterior dislocation)

tests: Posterior apprehension (flexion–adduction–internal rotation with posterior load)
structures: Posterior capsule, ischiofemoral ligament, ligamentum teres
keywords.mechanism: Posterior dislocation occurs when an axial force travels along the femoral shaft with the hip flexed and adducted, as when the knee strikes a car dashboard. The force levers the femoral head over the posterior acetabular rim, tearing the posterior capsule and labrum. With less flexion or more abduction at impact, the posterior wall of the acetabulum fractures (fracture-dislocation) [r1,r2]. Anterior dislocation results from forced abduction and external rotation, with the hip extended (pubic type) or flexed (obturator type) [r2].

name: Traumatic meniscal tear
populations: people with an acute ACL injury
manual workers who squat and twist
summary: An acute tear of the medial or lateral meniscus from twisting on a flexed, weight-bearing knee, causing joint-line pain, delayed swelling and sometimes catching or locking.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing knee flexion with rotation on a planted foot

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Joint-line tenderness (Sn 83%, Sp 83%); Thessaly 20° (Sn 75%, Sp 87%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI when surgery is being considered or the knee locks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean ~2 months after partial meniscectomy; ~6 months after repair

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Exercise-first care: clinically relevant improvement by 12 weeks to 12 months

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and adults under 40 in pivoting sport

grading: Tear pattern and vascular zone (arthroscopic/MRI description)

keywords.mechanism: The classic non-contact mechanism is rotation of the femur on a fixed tibia while the knee is flexed and loaded, for example twisting to change direction with the foot planted. Axial compression traps the meniscus between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau while rotation and anteroposterior translation shear it. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is least mobile and is the usual site; the lateral meniscus is more often torn at the time of an acute ACL rupture.

name: Traumatic rotator cuff tear
populations: adults in their 50s (mean about 55 years in one systematic review)
older adults after a fall or shoulder dislocation
summary: A sudden tear of one or more rotator cuff tendons after a fall or forceful pull, with immediate pain and weakness. It may be a new tear or an acute-on-chronic extension of a degenerate tendon.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months: about 6–12 months after repair (clinical convention); non-operative recovery is slower and less predictable for large tears

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; commonly not before about 6 months after repair, and 9–12 months for overhead or contact sport (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: External rotation lag sign (LR+ 7.2) and internal rotation lag sign (LR+ 5.6) for full-thickness tears

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound or MRI: sensitivity and specificity over 0.90 for full-thickness tears

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean about 55 years (systematic review of traumatic tears), largely male

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Fall onto the arm most common; subscapularis involved in 78% in the same review

grading: Descriptive classification by depth and size (no single universally accepted system)

structures: Rotator interval and long head of biceps
Long head of biceps and rotator interval
keywords.mechanism: A traumatic tear usually follows a fall onto the outstretched or abducted arm, or a sudden forceful pull, in which the cuff tendons are overloaded eccentrically while the arm is abducted and externally rotated [r1]. The load exceeds the tensile capacity of the tendon, which is often already degenerate. The failure typically starts in the supraspinatus near its footprint on the greater tuberosity and can extend posteriorly to infraspinatus and anteriorly to the rotator interval and subscapularis.

name: Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) injury
populations: people with a previous wrist or distal radius injury
summary: Tear or wear of the cartilage-and-ligament complex on the ulnar side of the wrist, causing ulnar-sided pain, clicking and sometimes distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) instability. Traumatic or degenerative.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Nonoperative care is a reasonable first step: a systematic review of 8 studies (427 wrists) found outcomes comparable to surgery, but randomised trials are lacking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ulnar fovea sign: sensitivity 95.2% and specificity 86.5% in one arthroscopy series of 272 patients, but it also picks up ulnotriquetral tears; most TFCC tests are not validated against arthroscopy

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Pooled MRI sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81 for full-thickness tears versus 0.84 and 0.95 for MR arthrography (21 studies, 982 wrists)

keyFacts.label: Healing capacity
keyFacts.value: Only the peripheral 10–40% of the TFCC has a blood supply, so peripheral tears can heal or be repaired but central tears are unlikely to heal

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. In one small racquet-sport series the average return to baseline activity was 134 days

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Palmer class 1 (traumatic) and class 2 (degenerative); foveal tears matter because they threaten DRUJ stability

grading: Palmer classification (traumatic class 1, degenerative class 2). Sub-class descriptions follow the classic scheme and are not drawn from a single abstract read

tests: Press test and DRUJ dorsopalmar stress test
differentials: Distal radius or ulnar styloid fracture
Triquetral fracture, pisotriquetral arthritis or DRUJ arthritis
keywords.mechanism: Traumatic tears typically follow a fall on the outstretched hand with the forearm pronated, or a rotational or distraction force through a gripped hand, for example a racquet or club striking the ground (clinical; mechanism as commonly described). Axial load drives the ulnar head toward the carpus while rotation stresses the radioulnar ligaments at their foveal and peripheral attachments [r1,r4]. Degenerative tears arise from repeated ulnocarpal loading, often in an ulnar-positive wrist, which wears the central disc and then the lunate and ulnar head cartilage [r12,r13].

name: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis)
populations: people in repetitive-gripping or vibrating-tool work
summary: Painful catching or locking of a finger or thumb because a thickened flexor tendon and A1 pulley no longer glide smoothly. Common in women, people with diabetes and repetitive gripping work.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Orthosis, injection or both gave resolution or improvement in 68.9% of 104 people in one trial; pooled injection success was 57% across four older RCTs

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Active composite fist with palpation of a tender A1 pulley nodule; grade with the Quinnell classification (grades 1–4)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed for a typical presentation; ultrasound-guided and blind injections did not differ significantly in a systematic review

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age 52–62 years in injection trials, with about 75% women

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Lifetime incidence of 2–3% reported

keyFacts.label: Risk setting
keyFacts.value: Diabetes: odds ratio 3.79 for trigger finger in a meta-analysis

grading: Quinnell classification of trigger finger severity (as defined in a large injection series)

tests: Passive extension of a locked digit
differentials: Palmar ganglion or flexor sheath mass
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury moment. Repeated or sustained forceful gripping presses the flexor tendons against the A1 pulley at the distal palmar crease, over the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint (clinical). Over time the pulley's gliding surface wears and is replaced by fibrous tissue [r2], and the flexor tendon develops a nodule or thickened segment, so the tendon and its tunnel no longer match in size. The nodule catches as it passes under the pulley when the digit flexes and again when it extends [r1].

name: Turf toe (1st MTP plantar plate injury)
aka: plantar plate complex injury of the great toe
populations: football players (American football, rugby and soccer), especially on firm or artificial surfaces
running backs and quarterbacks in college football (NCAA surveillance data)
dancers, gymnasts, wrestlers and martial artists
summary: A sprain of the 1st MTP plantar plate complex from forced hyperextension of the great toe, usually on a firm surface. Graded I to III; high-grade injuries risk instability, weak push-off and hallux rigidus.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I: back when pain-free with normal weightbearing (traditionally 3–5 days). Grade II: 2–4 weeks lost. Grade III: sources range from 4–6 weeks or more to at least 10–16 weeks, and up to 6 months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: NCAA football: mean 10.1 days lost per injury. Operative grade III series (15 football players): mean 16.5 weeks of playing time missed

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Painful, limited great-toe dorsiflexion with plantar tenderness after a hyperextension injury; the vertical Lachman test checks for instability

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weightbearing radiographs with comparison films (sesamoid retraction of 3 mm or more suggests plantar plate rupture); MRI to grade the tear

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Clanton and Ford grades I–III, as modified by McCormick and Anderson (sprain, partial tear, complete tear)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 0.062 per 1000 athlete-exposures in NCAA football; fewer than 2% of injuries need surgery

grading: Clanton and Ford grades I–III (modified by McCormick and Anderson)

tests: Vertical Lachman test of the first MTP joint
Varus and valgus stress of the first MTP joint
Isolated flexor hallucis brevis strength test
structures: Flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis and adductor hallucis
FHB, FHL and the adductor and abductor hallucis
differentials: Hallux sesamoid injury (fracture, stress fracture or sesamoiditis)
Hallux rigidus or first MTP arthritis
Gout or other inflammatory arthritis of the first MTP
Septic arthritis or infection of the first MTP
Proximal phalanx or first metatarsal head fracture
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is an axial load on a hyperextended first MTP joint with the ankle plantarflexed and the heel raised, so that the foot is fixed on the surface while the body continues forward, or another player lands on the athlete's heel [r1,r5]. The load forces the great toe into hyperextension beyond its normal range. The plantar plate complex, which resists dorsiflexion, is stretched and then fails, most often distal to the sesamoids at its firm attachment to the base of the proximal phalanx [r1]. Depending on the force direction, the injury can involve the medial or lateral structures and the sesamoids [r1].

name: Whiplash-associated disorder
aka: neck strain after motor vehicle crash
populations: drivers and passengers in motor vehicle collisions
people with high initial pain, disability or post-traumatic stress (higher risk of slow recovery)
summary: Neck pain and related symptoms after a sudden acceleration-deceleration of the neck, usually a rear-end collision. The pain source is often uncertain. Many recover, but a substantial minority do not.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve over weeks to months (median self-reported recovery 59–108 days across arms of one grade I–II trial), but about 50% still report neck pain at 1 year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated whiplash-specific criteria. Needs pain-free active rotation, no neurological signs and near-normal Neck Disability Index scores

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Canadian C-spine rule first, to exclude fracture: sensitivity 99.4–100% in alert, stable trauma patients. Then classify by Quebec Task Force grade

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Used to exclude fracture or instability when the Canadian C-spine rule is positive; it does not usually identify the pain source

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adults of all ages; age 35 or older and high initial disability predict slower recovery

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Varies substantially between countries; emergency department visits for WAD have risen over 30 years in the Western world

grading: Quebec Task Force classification of WAD (grades 0–IV) [r1]

structures: Deep neck flexors (longus colli, longus capitis)
Third occipital nerve and greater occipital nerve
C2–3 joint and third occipital nerve
differentials: Thoracic outlet or brachial plexus injury
keywords.mechanism: WAD follows a rapid acceleration-deceleration of the neck, classically when a stationary or slow-moving car is struck from behind. The seat accelerates the trunk forward while the head lags behind, so the neck is driven into relative extension. The head then rebounds into flexion. In a sled study of ten healthy male volunteers (4 km/h) filmed with cineradiography, the neck did not extend as one smooth curve: C6 rotated backward first and C5 followed, while the upper segments went into flexion, giving an S-shaped neck with 'open-book' motion at C5–6 [r10].
